t: Small, steady power from water, wind, muscle and stove heat: enough for lights, a radio and phones. Below you'll find honest numbers, simple builds, and the wiring and safety rules that stop you burning the place down. For emergencies and learning. At 12 V a shock is unlikely, but batteries can start fires, and some home-built generators make voltages that can kill. Anything connected to house wiring or the grid is a job for a licensed electrician. Two rules that save lives Never back-feed a house through an outlet (a "suicide cord"). It can electrocute line workers and neighbours. Use a properly installed transfer switch or interlock. Never run a fuel generator, stove, heater or grill inside a home, garage, tent, snow shelter or vehicle. Carbon monoxide kills. Keep generators at least 20 ft (6 m) from doors and windows, with the exhaust pointed away.

List daily needs. 2 phone charges (2 × 15 Wh = 30 Wh) + 2 LED lamps at 3 W for 5 h (30 Wh) + radio at 1 W for 5 h (5 Wh) = 65 Wh. Add about 30% for losses (wires, battery, converters): 65 × 1.3 ≈ 85 Wh per day. Battery for 2 days with no input: 2 × 85 = 170 Wh usable. Lead-acid (use only the top half): 340 Wh ÷ 12 V ≈ 28 Ah, so buy a 35 Ah or bigger deep-cycle battery. LiFePO4 (use about 80%): 213 Wh ÷ 12.8 V ≈ 17 Ah, so a 20 Ah pack. Generation to match 85 Wh/day: a hydro setup giving just 3.5 W around the clock, or about 2.5 hours of pedalling at 50 W, or a 1.5 m wind turbine on a steadily breezy day.

DC (direct current) flows one way. Batteries, solar panels, USB and cars are DC. AC (alternating current) reverses many times a second. House mains are AC: 120 V 60 Hz in North America, 230 V 50 Hz in Europe. Many home-built generators make AC, or a "wild" DC that rises and falls with speed. It must be rectified and regulated before it touches a battery. Turning battery DC into mains AC needs an inverter, which wastes power. Run things on DC wherever you can.

Car, boat and RV parts all run on 12 V: batteries, lights, fans, radios, USB chargers, fuses, switches. You can scavenge them almost anywhere. 12 V is very unlikely to shock you through dry skin. The danger is fire from short circuits. Downside: low voltage means high current for the same power, so wires must be thick and short. 1,000 W is about 83 A at 12 V, but only about 8 A at 120 V. Bigger systems use 24 V or 48 V to keep currents down.

Falling or flowing water spins a wheel or turbine. The wheel spins a generator (usually a permanent-magnet DC motor run backwards). If you have a stream with some drop, this is the best option on this page because it runs 24 hours a day. Just 50 W around the clock is 1.2 kWh per day, far more than you could ever pedal.

h: How much power? Head and flow
f: How much power? Head and flow
t: Head is the vertical drop from where you take the water to the turbine. Flow is how much water goes through, in litres per second. Power (W) ≈ 9.81 × flow (L/s) × head (m) × efficiency For efficiency, use 0.5 for a decent improvised build. Use 0.3 for a crude wheel with several belt stages. (1 L/s ≈ 16 US gal/min. 1 m ≈ 3.3 ft.) Worked example A 10 L bucket fills from your pipe in about 7 seconds, so flow ≈ 1.5 L/s. The pipe drops 8 m (26 ft). Power ≈ 9.81 × 1.5 × 8 × 0.5 ≈ 59 W. Over 24 hours that's about 1.4 kWh per day, plenty for lights, phones, a radio and a laptop. Head is the vertical drop from the intake's water surface to the turbine. It is not the length of the pipe.

Small stream (bucket method): Run the whole flow, or the share you'll use, through a pipe into a bucket of known size. Time how long it takes to fill. Flow (L/s) = litres ÷ seconds. Do it 3 times and average. Bigger stream (float method): Pick a straight 10 m stretch. Measure the average width and depth in metres. Time a floating stick over the 10 m. Flow (L/s) ≈ width × depth × (10 ÷ seconds) × 0.8 × 1,000. Measure in the dry season and design for the lowest flow. Plan to take only a share of the stream.

Hold a straight board or pole level (check it with a spirit level), one end on the slope, pointing downhill. Measure straight down from the far end to the ground. That is one step of drop. Move to that spot and repeat all the way down from the intake to the turbine site. Add up the steps. Phone altimeters and GPS are too inaccurate for drops of a few metres. Pipe friction eats some head. Use pipe big enough that you lose no more than about 10–15% of it, and go bigger if in doubt. As a rough guide, 2 in (50 mm) pipe suits about 1–2 L/s over a run of up to about 50 m (160 ft).

Type Best for Notes Pelton / Turgo runner (jet from a nozzle hits cups on a disc) Several metres of head or more, small flow Fast and efficient. Often drives the generator directly. Cups can be cut from split pipe or made from steel spoons. Overshot wheel (water poured onto the top) A drop about as tall as the wheel, more flow Can be efficient if well built, but slow (often 5–30 rpm). Needs big step-up gearing. Undershot wheel (paddles dipped in a current) Flat streams with no drop Very weak. A stream moving at walking pace (about 1 m/s) gives only about 15–30 W from a crude wheel with about 0.3 m² (3 sq ft) of paddle in the water. For example, a motor labelled 130 V at 5,000 rpm needs about 540 rpm to make 14 V, plus a bit more to push current into a battery. h: Why a car alternator is a poor choice
f: Why a car alternator is a poor choice
t: It needs roughly 1,000–2,000+ rpm at the alternator shaft before it charges usefully. In a car the belt spins it 2–3 times faster than the engine. A 1.5 m rotor turns only about 250–350 rpm in a 5 m/s breeze. It has no permanent magnets. Its rotor is an electromagnet that needs field (excitation) current, a few amps from your battery, before it makes anything. In light wind it can use more than it makes. Gearing it up 5:1 or more adds friction and losses, and the rotor then struggles to start. Alternators suit engine drives or a fast Pelton runner. For wind, use a permanent-magnet motor.

Treadmill motors (often rated about 90–130 V DC at several thousand rpm) reach 12–14 V at a few hundred to about 1,000 rpm. That's a reasonable match for a small rotor with direct drive and no gearbox. Washing-machine direct-drive motors are another popular choice. See scavenging. Wind safety Blade throw: a broken blade can fly a long way. Never stand in line with the spinning rotor. Keep people and animals out of the area around the tower. Tower falls: keep everyone out of a circle at least 1.5× the tower height while raising, lowering or in storms. Check anchors and guys. Runaway: a turbine with no load overspeeds until blades break. Never leave it disconnected from a load in wind. Use a diversion (dump-load) controller. Never use a solar controller that simply disconnects. Storms: stop it before a storm, while the wind is still moderate. Close the brake switch (it shorts the generator, which brakes it hard), then tie the rotor or lower the tower. Shorting at full speed can burn the brake switch or motor. High voltage: treadmill motors spinning fast with no load can make well over 60 V DC, enough to give a dangerous shock.

t: A bike on a stand drives a permanent-magnet DC motor, which charges a battery. It's reliable and works in any weather, but human muscles are weak engines. Realistic output Fit adult: about 75–100 W sustained. Most people: about 50 W over an hour. After losses that's roughly 30–70 Wh stored per hour, or about 2 phone charges per hour at 50 W. Hand crank: 5–20 W, and arms tire fast. Fine for a radio or LED, but only part of a phone charge. Pedal and crank safety Entanglement: rollers, belts and chains grab hair, laces, drawstrings and loose sleeves. Guard them, tie back hair, and keep children and pets away. Blocking diode or rectifier is not optional. Without it, the battery drives the motor when you stop pedalling. Regulate for USB. Raw generator output swings with speed and will destroy phones. Always charge through a battery and a proper 12 V → USB buck converter. A treadmill motor spun fast with nothing connected can exceed 60 V. Treat its terminals as live.

t: Lift the back wheel on a trainer stand and make it rock-solid. It must not tip when you stand on the pedals. Mount the motor on a hinged bracket so a spring or bungee presses its roller firmly against the tyre. Or run a belt from the rim to a pulley on the motor. Check the speed. At a comfortable 60–80 pedal rpm, the motor should give about 14–18 V with nothing connected. Measure with a meter. Change the roller or pulley size if it's too low or too high. Add a flywheel. A heavy flywheel on the motor, or the trainer's own, smooths out the pulses of each pedal stroke. Wire it: motor + → blocking diode → controller input +; motor − → controller input −. Controller battery terminals → fuse → battery. Connect the battery to the controller first. Fit the meter so you can see the watts you're making. Run phones from the battery through the 12 V → USB converter. Never connect a phone straight to the motor. Pedal in steady 20–30 minute sessions and drink water. Pedalling burns water and food, so weigh that cost in a crisis.

h: Thermoelectric power from a wood stove
t: A thermoelectric generator (TEG) module is a thin ceramic tile. Heat one face and cool the other, and it makes a small DC voltage (the Seebeck effect). It has no moving parts and runs whenever the stove burns, but the output is small. The temperature difference (ΔT) is everything. Power rises roughly with the square of ΔT: double the difference gives about 4× the power. A hot stove is only half the job. The cold side must stay cold. TEG vs Peltier (TEC): Peltier cooler modules (TEC) also work as generators in a pinch. They're built for cooling, though, so they usually tolerate much less heat (their solder can melt well below stove-top temperatures) and give less power. Buy modules sold as TEGs if you can. Hot-side limit: many common bismuth-telluride modules are rated for a hot side of about 150–250 °C (300–480 °F). Check the specific module and never exceed it. A wood stove top can run hotter than that. Realistic output One 40 mm module with an air-cooled heat sink on a wood stove typically gives about 0.5–3 W. Commercial stove-top thermoelectric chargers are typically rated about 5–20 W. Over a day of burning that's roughly 10–200 Wh: a slow phone charge and some LED light. Stack: stove → thick aluminium spreader → paste → TEG → paste → heat sink. The bigger the temperature difference, the more power. Stove safety Carbon monoxide: a wood stove must vent through a proper flue. Fit a CO alarm. Never bring a grill, camp stove or heater indoors to run a thermoelectric charger. …

h: Earth battery, voltaic pile and lemon cells
t: Two different metals (zinc and copper) in a salty or acidic electrolyte make a small battery. These are fun and educational, but be honest about what you'll get. Honest expectations About 0.5–1 V per cell, at microamps to a few milliamps. Red LED needs about 1.8–2 V: 3–4 cells in series. White LED needs about 3 V: 4–6 cells. Expect a dim glow. An LCD clock or calculator (microamps) can run for a while. It cannot charge a phone in any useful time. A phone charges at 5–20 W. A lemon cell gives under a thousandth of a watt. You'd need thousands of cells. Each cell is zinc | wet paper | copper. The copper of one cell touches the zinc of the next, so the cells add up in series.

Connect an LED's long leg to +. If it doesn't light, add cells. Re-wet the paper when the output fades. Replace badly corroded discs.

h: How to test any motor as a generator
t: Look at it. Two wires usually means a brushed DC motor. Three thick wires means a brushless 3-phase motor. Four to six thin wires usually means a stepper. Short test: twist the leads together (all three for 3-phase) and turn the shaft by hand. If it gets much harder to turn than with the leads apart, it has magnets and will generate. No change means no magnets. Voltage test: separate the leads. Set a multimeter to DC volts (AC volts for brushless, stepper and dynamo types). Spin the shaft at a steady, known speed (for example with a drill in the chuck) and read the open-circuit volts. Voltage rises roughly in step with rpm. Load test (the real number): connect a load, such as a 12 V car bulb (5–21 W) or a power resistor. Measure the volts across it and the amps through it. Watts = volts × amps. Open-circuit volts always look better than real output. Work out the gearing you need to reach about 14–15 V under load at the speed your wheel, rotor or pedals can give. Testing safety Clamp the motor down before spinning it with a drill. Keep fingers, sleeves and hair clear of the chuck. High-voltage motors (treadmill motors) spun fast can exceed 60 V, so keep the leads apart and don't touch them.

Wire it right and it's safe. Wire it wrong and the battery becomes a fire-starter. Follow this order: Power flows top to bottom. Fuses go on the battery's positive side, as close to the battery as possible.

A bridge rectifier (4 diodes in one block) turns AC, or DC of either polarity, into DC. Use a 3-phase bridge (6 diodes) for 3-phase motors and alternators. Rate it for at least twice your maximum current and well above the highest voltage your generator can make. Metal-cased 35 A bridges are cheap and common. A silicon bridge drops about 1.4 V (two diodes in the path). At 12 V that's over 10% lost as heat. At 10 A it makes about 14 W of heat, so bolt it to a metal heat sink with thermal paste.

It stops the battery pushing current back into the generator and spinning it as a motor (or draining the battery) when the generator slows or stops. Use a Schottky diode (only about 0.3–0.5 V lost), rated for at least twice your current and well above your generator's maximum voltage. Heat-sink it. A bridge rectifier already blocks back-flow, so you don't need both.

Why you need one: overcharging boils lead-acid batteries dry, gives off lots of hydrogen and kills them. Overcharged lithium packs can catch fire. Running any battery flat also ruins it. PWM: cheap and simple. Works best when the source voltage is only a little above the battery's. MPPT: converts a higher source voltage down efficiently. It harvests noticeably more (often 10–30% with solar) when the source voltage is well above the battery's. Wind and hydro: use a diversion (dump-load) controller. When the battery is full, it sends surplus power into a dump load (a heating element or power resistors) instead of disconnecting the generator. The turbine always stays loaded and can't run away. Rate the dump load for more than the generator's maximum output, and mount it where its heat is safe. Solar-type controllers that disconnect are fine for solar and pedal only. Low-voltage disconnect: use the controller's LOAD output or a separate disconnect so lights and gadgets can't drain the battery flat. Connect the battery to the controller first, then the generator. Disconnect in reverse order.

Lead-acid deep-cycle (flooded, AGM, gel): cheap, heavy and forgiving. For long life, use only the top half: don't go below about 50%. Recharge fully and often; leaving one discharged ruins it. Flooded types need distilled-water top-ups and vent the most hydrogen. A flat lead-acid battery can freeze and crack in winter. Car starting batteries die quickly if discharged deeply. Use one only in an emergency. LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate): lighter, about 80–90% usable, long life. It must have a BMS (battery management system). Don't charge it below 0 °C (32 °F) unless it has built-in low-temperature protection or a heater. Other lithium packs (phone, laptop, power-tool, e-bike): charge only with their own chargers. Don't connect home-built generators to them. 12 V battery Charging voltages Notes Flooded lead-acid Absorb: about 14.4–14.8 V Float: about 13.2–13.6 V Resting (2+ h, no load): 12.6–12.7 V ≈ full; about 12.2 V ≈ half; under 12.0 V ≈ nearly empty, so recharge now. AGM / gel Per the label (usually a bit lower; gel lowest) Overcharging dries them out permanently. LiFePO4 Absorb: about 14.2–14.6 V Float: not needed, or per the maker BMS required. Voltage stays almost flat until nearly empty, so it's a poor fuel gauge. Always follow the battery's own spec when you have it.

Distance is one-way (the cable length from battery to device). Use stranded copper. Fuse every battery positive lead as close to the battery as possible (within about 7 in / 18 cm). A fuse protects the wire from melting and burning. DC arcs harder than AC, and an AC-only switch can weld shut or burn. Fit a battery disconnect switch you can reach quickly. Red = positive, black = negative. That can be up to 0.6 kWh a day doing nothing, which is enough to flatten a small battery. Switch it off when not in use. Big current: a 1,000 W load pulls about 90–100 A from a 12 V battery. Pure sine wave is safest for electronics, motors and medical devices. Modified sine wave can make some devices overheat or fail. Inverter output is mains voltage and can kill. Treat it like a wall socket. Never connect an inverter to house wiring through an outlet.

Fit the battery fuse holders with the fuses out. Connect the controller to the battery (through the fuse holder), then the dump load if you have one. Connect the generator through the rectifier or diode with the generator stopped (water off, rotor tied, pedals still). Check polarity with a meter at every point, then insert the fuses. Shock DC above about 50–60 V, and any mains AC, can kill. Treadmill motors spun fast, and solar panels wired in series, can easily exceed this. Work on circuits only when they're dead: generator stopped, battery fuse out. Use one hand where possible and keep the other away from metal. Short circuits and fire A 12 V battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a short. That melts wrenches, welds rings and watches to terminals, and causes severe burns. Remove rings, watches and metal bracelets. Insulate tool handles. Cover battery terminals. Fuse every battery positive lead as close to the battery as possible. Make the final connection at the fuse or switch, never with a spark at the terminal. Wear goggles and gloves. Neutralize acid spills with baking soda. t: Lay out Symbol Meaning V Require assistance X Require medical assistance N No / negative Y Yes / affirmative Arrow Proceeding in this direction (point it the way you are going) Make each symbol at least 10 ft (3 m) tall — bigger is better — with thick, straight lines. Use strong contrast: dark branches or rocks on snow or sand, bright fabric on dark ground, or trenches that cast shadows. Build in the most open place nearby, away from tree cover. Straight lines and sharp angles rarely occur in nature, so they catch the eye. SOS or HELP in large letters is also widely understood. To a helicopter or aircraft: both arms raised in a Y = "Yes, we need help". One arm up and one down (like an N) = "No, we don't need help". Don't wave casually at aircraft — it can be misread. Note: Distress Three of anything = distress: 3 fires (in a triangle or a line), 3 whistle blasts, 3 horn blasts, 3 flashes of light, 3 shots, 3 piles of rocks.

3 blasts = help. Blow 3 long blasts, pause about a minute, listen, repeat. In European mountains you may hear the alpine distress signal: 6 blasts in a minute, a minute's pause, repeat; the reply is 3 blasts a minute. Answer either one. A whistle carries much farther than a voice and uses far less energy.

SOS = 3 short, 3 long, 3 short, then a pause; repeat. Timing: short flash about 1 count, long flash 3 counts, 1 count dark between flashes, 3 counts between letters, 7 counts or more before repeating. A count is about half a second. Slow and steady is easier to read than fast. Aim at the aircraft, boat or distant observer.

Hold the mirror close under your eye. Stretch your other arm toward the target (aircraft, ship, vehicle) and make a V with two fingers, with the target in the V. Tilt the mirror until the spot of sunlight it reflects lands on your fingers. Keep the light spot on your fingers and the target inside the V — the flash is now hitting the target. Rock the mirror slightly so the flash sweeps across the target. A signal mirror with a sighting hole: look through the hole and put its bright aiming spot on the target. Sweep the horizon now and then even when you see nothing — a flash can be seen from many miles away. Once they have seen you, stop flashing directly at the cockpit.

Phones: in many places, dialling 911 or 112 works on any phone with any network in range — not just your own — and in many countries even without a SIM card. Try it even when the phone shows "No service" or "Emergency calls only". Texts often get through when calls don't. In the US you can text 911 in many areas (you get a bounce-back message if not). Some newer phones can send emergency messages by satellite — learn how before you go. PLB / satellite messenger: extend the antenna, keep a clear view of the sky, activate and leave it on. Marine VHF: channel 16 (156.8 MHz) is the distress, safety and calling channel. On a DSC radio, hold the red DISTRESS button for a few seconds first. "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" = grave and imminent danger to life or vessel. "PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN" = urgent, but not immediately life-threatening. Then: "This is" + vessel/name 3 times; your position; what is wrong; help needed; number of people; "Over". Repeat if no answer. Other radios: in the US, CB channel 9 is for emergencies and traveller assistance. 121.5 MHz is the aviation emergency frequency.

Practise each knot with real cord at home, until you can tie it with cold hands and your eyes closed.

s: A fixed loop that won't slip or jam — around a tree, a post, a person in a rescue.
t: Make a small loop in the standing part, with the working end side lying on top. Pass the working end up through the small loop from underneath. Take it around behind the standing part. Bring it back down through the small loop. Hold the working end against the big loop and pull the standing part to tighten. Leave a tail at least 10–12 rope-widths long. Caution Can shake loose when not under load — back it up with a stopper knot.

s: An adjustable loop for tent and tarp guy-lines; slides to tighten, holds under load.
t: Pass the working end around the stake or anchor. Wrap it twice around the standing part, working inside the loop toward the anchor. Bring it out past the two wraps and make one more turn around the standing part, outside the loop. Tuck the end under that last turn and pull snug. Slide the knot along the line to adjust the tension. Caution Can slip on slick or stiff modern cord — test it before trusting it.

s: Quick hitch to a post, pole or tree; starting point for lashings.
t: Wrap the working end once around the post. Cross it over the standing part and wrap around the post again, forming an X. Tuck the end under the second wrap, so both ends come out of the middle of the X, in opposite directions. Pull both ends to tighten. Caution Slips when the load changes direction or the post rotates — add two half hitches for security.

s: Binding knot: tying off bandages, slings and bundles.
t: Right over left and under. Left over right and under. Check: both loops lie flat and match, and each end lies alongside its own standing part. (If not, it's a granny knot — retie.) Caution Not for joining two ropes that will carry a load — it can spill apart.

s: A friction hitch that grips a rope under load and slides when loose — ascending, hauling, tensioning lines.
t: Make a closed loop of cord thinner than the main rope. Lay the loop behind the main rope and pass it through itself around the rope. Repeat so the cord wraps the rope 3 times, each pass going through the loop. Dress the wraps neat and parallel, with no crossings; the loop comes out of the middle. Load the loop to make it grip; push the knot (not the loop) to slide it. Caution Climbing, rescue or any life-safety use needs proper training and equipment.

Call 911 / 112 early. Protect yourself first. These are reminders — take a hands-on course. More detail: First Aid page. Note: Medicines Pain relief (adults): follow the package label. Acetaminophen/paracetamol: no more than 3,000 mg a day without a doctor's advice (label max 4,000 mg; liver risk, avoid alcohol). Ibuprofen: 200–400 mg every 4–6 hours, max 1,200 mg a day unless a doctor directs (stomach bleeding and kidney risk; avoid when dehydrated). No aspirin for under-19s (Reye's syndrome).

Protect yourself (gloves if you have them). Call or send for help: 911 / 112. Press firmly and directly on the wound with a dressing or cloth. Pack deep wounds with gauze or cloth and keep pressing hard. Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure: apply a tourniquet 2–3 in (5–7 cm) above the wound, not on a joint ("high and tight" on the limb if you can't see where it is coming from). Tighten until the bleeding stops. It will hurt — that is expected. Note the time (write it on the tourniquet or skin). Do NOT loosen it once applied. Get to emergency care. Keep the person warm and lying down; treat for shock. Improvised tourniquet: a wide band (not wire or thin cord) tightened with a stick as a windlass, then the stick secured.

Safe to approach? Not responsive and not breathing normally (gasping is not normal)? Call 911 / 112 (speaker on) and send someone for an AED. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest: 100–120 per minute, at least 2 in (5 cm) but not more than 2.4 in (6 cm) deep, letting the chest fully recoil. If trained and willing: 30 compressions : 2 breaths. Otherwise hands-only — keep pushing without stopping. Use the AED as soon as it arrives: switch it on and follow its voice prompts. Keep going until help takes over, the person starts breathing normally, or you are too exhausted or in danger.

Can they cough or speak? Encourage them to keep coughing. Adult or child over 1 year who can't cough, speak or breathe: 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts. Repeat. Infant under 1 year: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (two fingers, centre of chest). Never abdominal thrusts. Becomes unresponsive: call 911 / 112 and start CPR. Anyone who received abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor afterwards.

Stop the burning. Cool with cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible. Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn unless it is stuck to the skin. No ice, butter or toothpaste. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy dressing. Keep the person warm. Get medical care for burns that are large or deep; on the face, hands, genitals or airway; or electrical or chemical burns.

Signs: shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech, confusion. Shivering that stops while they are still cold is a bad sign — get help. Handle gently. Get out of wind and wet; remove wet clothing and replace with dry layers. Insulate from the ground and cover the head. Warm the core — armpits, chest, groin — with warm packs, warm bottles wrapped in cloth, or body-to-body contact. Warm sweet drinks only if fully alert and able to swallow. No alcohol. Don't rub the limbs.

Hot + confused, collapsed or very drowsy = heat stroke — an emergency. Call 911 / 112. Cool immediately and aggressively. Cold-water immersion (up to the neck) is best. If you can't immerse: soak with water and fan hard; cold packs to neck, armpits and groin; shade. Give sips of cool water only if fully alert. Keep cooling until help arrives or they are clearly recovering. Heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, weakness, headache, nausea, still thinking clearly): rest in shade, cool down, sip water. Getting confused? Treat it as heat stroke.

Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; fast breathing; anxious, confused or drowsy. Call 911 / 112. Treat the cause — stop the bleeding. Lay them flat. If there is no injury to the legs, hips, spine or head, you may raise the legs about 12 in (30 cm). Keep them warm — insulate from the ground; loosen tight clothing. Nothing to eat or drink unless fully alert and help is many hours away (then small sips of water). Reassure them; check breathing often.

For someone unresponsive but breathing normally. Kneel beside them. Place the arm nearest you at a right angle to the body, palm up. Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek. With your other hand, lift the far knee so the foot is flat, then pull on the knee to roll them toward you onto their side. Bend the top leg so hip and knee are at right angles. Tilt the head back gently so the airway stays open and fluids can drain. Check breathing continuously. If it stops or becomes abnormal: call and start CPR. Keep them warm.

The printed PDF has a fill-in box on page 1 (name, date of birth, blood type, allergies, medications, conditions, emergency contacts) and a ruled page 17 for ICE contacts, meeting points and waypoints. Fill them in by hand in pencil or waterproof pen. In the app, you can also save waypoints on the Map page.

Print it now, before you need it. It is laid out for US Letter and also fits A4 (choose "Actual size" or "Fit to page"). Black-and-white printing is fine. Fill in page 1 and the contacts and waypoints page by hand, in pencil or waterproof pen. Update them once a year. Keep copies where emergencies happen: go-bag, vehicle glovebox, first-aid kit, near your home's main water and power shut-offs. Store each in a zip-top bag. In an emergency: start at page 1 — call for help, STOP, follow the priorities — then turn to your scenario using the quick-action index. Steps are numbered in the order that usually matters most. Adapt them to what you see — your own safety comes first. Read it through once now, and practise: knots, mirror signalling, map and compass. Take a first-aid and CPR course. The app's Emergency page has the same content, works offline, and may have a newer edition. Disclaimer. This guide gives general information for emergencies. It is not medical advice and is not a substitute for training, professional medical care, or instructions from emergency services and local authorities — always follow official orders. Situations differ: use your judgement. Figures are typical values from the sources below; always check product labels and local rules. Use at your own risk. Based on public guidance from: CDC (drinking water, carbon monoxide, generators), USDA (food safety in power outages), NWS/NOAA (floods, lightning, winter travel), FEMA / Ready.gov, American Red Cross …
x: heart association cal fire wildfire evacuation icao annex ground air signals international marine radio procedures

t: Get out of wind and wet first. Get off the cold ground. Then make fire. Every method below is numbered so you can follow it with cold hands. Read this first: practise these skills before you need them. Fire can kill you through burns, wildfire or carbon monoxide. Obey local fire bans. Knots here are for camp use — anything that holds a person's weight (climbing, rescue, lowering) needs proper training and rated gear.

Rule of 3s (typical, not absolute): you can last about 3 minutes without air (or in icy water, or with severe bleeding) 3 hours without shelter in harsh weather 3 days without water 3 weeks without food So in cold, wet or windy weather, shelter usually comes before fire. A fire can be rained out, burn down while you sleep, or run out of fuel. A good shelter keeps working all night. Stay dry. Wet clothing loses most of its insulation and pulls heat from you fast. Avoid sweating: slow down and open layers before you get hot. Get out of the wind. Use terrain, thick trees, boulders, or your pack and gear as a windbreak. Insulate from the ground. This matters more than a roof over your head. Cold ground steals heat far faster than cold air. Pile up a thick, springy bed of dry leaves, pine needles, grass or boughs — at least a hand-span thick once compressed. Then overhead cover, then fire. Fire is for warmth, drying out, boiling water, signalling and morale. Tip Collect everything — insulation, fuel, water — before dark. Night work in the cold is slow, clumsy and dangerous.

Danger — wet rocks can explode Never build a fire ring from wet, porous or river-bed rocks. Water trapped inside turns to steam and the rock can crack violently and throw hot fragments. Use dry rocks from high ground, or no ring at all. Do not sleep right against a rock face you have heated: it can flake off (spall). Check the rules. Obey fire bans and restrictions. In a true emergency, keep the fire as small as will do the job. Clear a circle of about 10 ft (3 m) down to bare mineral soil: no leaves, needles, dry grass or roots that can carry fire. Look up. No overhanging branches, dry foliage or tarps above the fire. Avoid peat, deep duff and root mats. Fire can creep underground and pop up later, metres away. Mind the wind. Sparks travel downwind. Put the fire downwind of your shelter and gear, and do not light it in strong wind. Keep water, a pot of soil or a shovel ready before you light anything. Never leave a fire unattended — not even for a few minutes.

Drown it with water (or damp soil if water is scarce — not dry leaves). Stir the ashes and embers, scrape partly burnt sticks, and drown again. Feel with the back of your hand just above, then on, the ashes. If anything is warm, repeat. If it's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave.

Fire needs heat, fuel and air. Most failures: wet fuel, too-big fuel, or smothering it (no air). End-on view of fuel thickness. Do not jump sizes. Stage Size Examples Tinder Fluffy, hair-fine Birch bark, dry grass, cattail fluff, shredded inner bark, wood shavings, cotton balls with petroleum jelly, char cloth Kindling Pencil-lead to pencil thick Dead twigs that snap cleanly, feather sticks, split sticks Small fuel Thumb thick Dead branches, split wood Fuel Wrist thick and up Add only once the fire is strong and has a bed of coals Gather twice what you think Before you strike anything, gather at least twice the tinder and kindling you think you need, sorted by size within arm's reach. Fires usually die in the first two minutes because the next size wasn't ready.

Standing dead wood and dead branches still on trees — drier than anything on the ground. If it bends instead of snapping, it's too wet. Split it. The core of a wet stick is often dry. Split wrist-thick dead wood with a knife and a baton. Feather sticks: shave thin curls down a dry split stick, leaving them attached. They catch like tinder. Birch bark (papery outer bark) burns even when damp — peel it from dead or fallen trees where you can. Fatwood: resin-soaked wood from dead pine stumps and branch joints. Smells of turpentine; shavings light even when wet. Dry grass, cattail fluff, old man's beard lichen — dry inside your clothing if damp. From your kit: cotton balls smeared with petroleum jelly (pull apart before lighting), char cloth, wax, hand sanitiser (alcohol gel — burns with a near-invisible flame). Build on a platform of dry sticks laid side by side, not on wet ground or snow.

c: Fire basics › Dry fuel in wet weather
s: catches a spark from flint & steel or a ferro rod
f: Make char cloth catches a spark from flint & steel or a ferro rod
t: Cut 100% cotton (old jeans, T-shirt, flannel) into squares about 2 in (5 cm). Synthetics melt — they won't work. Put them in a small metal tin with a lid (mint or shoe-polish tin). Punch one small hole in the lid with a nail. Put the tin in a fire or on coals. Smoke and gas will jet from the hole — sometimes alight. That's normal. When the smoke stops (often 5–10 minutes), remove the tin and let it cool completely before opening. Plug the hole with a twig while it cools so air can't get in. Good char cloth is black all through and flexible, not brown (undercooked) or crumbling to ash (overcooked). Store it dry in the tin.

Carry three ways to light a fire (e.g. lighter, ferro rod, waterproof matches) and dry tinder in a sealed bag. The methods below are for when those fail. All of them make an ember or spark that you grow in a tinder bundle: Make a fist-sized "bird's nest" of fine, dry tinder: coarser material outside, finest fibres in the middle. Put the ember or burning material in the centre and fold the nest loosely around it. Hold it up, below and upwind of your face, and blow gently and steadily. Smoke thickens, then it flames. Place it at once under your kindling (already laid — see fire lays).

s: most reliable; works wet, in wind and at altitude
f: Ferro rod (ferrocerium) most reliable; works wet, in wind and at altitude
t: New rods have a black coating — scrape it off first until you get sparks. Prepare a tinder bundle, cotton-and-petroleum-jelly ball, fatwood shavings or birch bark shavings on a dry base. Put the rod tip right in or against the tinder. Hold the striker (or the 90° spine of a knife — never the cutting edge) still, pressing firmly on the rod at a steep angle. Pull the rod back toward you while the striker stays put. This keeps your hand from smashing the tinder and puts sparks exactly where you aimed. Use slow, firm, full-length scrapes. Once the tinder catches, feed kindling.

s: friction fire — hard work; practise in good conditions first
f: Bow drill friction fire — hard work; practise in good conditions first
t: Left: the set from the side. Right: the notch, cut after burning in the depression. Wood: dead, bone-dry, fairly soft wood — cedar, willow, poplar/aspen/cottonwood, basswood (linden), yucca stalk. Using the same wood for spindle and fireboard usually works. Your thumbnail should just dent it. Spindle: straight, about thumb-thick and a hand-span long (roughly 2 cm × 20 cm). Round the bottom; point the top slightly. Fireboard: flat, about finger-thick (1.5–2 cm), wider than the spindle. Bow: a stiff stick about arm-length with cord (shoelace, paracord) tied so the spindle twists into it tightly. Bearing block: hardwood, stone with a dimple, or bone. Lubricate its socket (grease, soap, lip balm, crushed green leaves) so friction happens at the bottom, not the top. Kneel, foot on the board, wrist braced against your shin so the spindle stays vertical. Burn a shallow depression near the board's edge. Cut the notch: a V from the board's edge to the centre of the depression, about 1/8 of the circle. Put a dry leaf or bark under it. Drill with long, full strokes using the whole bow. Start steady, then add speed and downward pressure as smoke builds and dark powder fills the notch. When there is heavy smoke and the powder keeps smoking on its own, stop. Let it sit a few seconds; fan gently. Tap the board and lift it away. Move the ember on its leaf/bark into the tinder bundle and blow gently until it flames. Caution This takes a lot of energy and sweat. In the cold, sweat chills you …
x: work short bursts open layers don any other option

s: only in strong, direct sun
f: Lens (sunlight) only in strong, direct sun
t: Lens options: magnifying glass; reading glasses with strong magnifying (positive) lenses — glasses for short-sightedness will not work; a clear water-filled bottle or clear plastic bag twisted into a ball; or a lens shaped from very clear ice, smoothed with warm hands (cloudy ice will not work). Use dark tinder — char cloth, punky wood, or tinder blackened with charcoal catches far faster. Angle the lens square to the sun. Move it toward and away from the tinder until the spot is the smallest, brightest point. Hold it perfectly still and shield it from wind. When it glows, transfer to a tinder bundle and blow gently. Don't stare at the bright spot for long. Midday sun works best; hazy or low sun often fails.

s: fast and easy if you carry both
f: Battery + steel wool fast and easy if you carry both
t: Use fine steel wool (grade 0000). Fluff out a pad on top of your tinder bundle. 9 V battery: touch both terminals to the wool at the same time. It glows and spreads instantly. AA / D cells: hold two or more end to end (+ to −), and touch a thin strip of wool across the two free ends. Fold the tinder around the glowing wool and blow gently. Fire risk in your pack Store steel wool sealed, away from batteries (separate bag or tin). A 9 V battery touching loose steel wool in a pack can start a fire.

s: flint & steel, fire piston, chemical
f: Other methods flint & steel, fire piston, chemical
t: Flint & steel: strike a high-carbon steel striker down along the sharp edge of a hard rock (flint, chert, quartz) with char cloth held on top of the rock. Sparks land on the cloth and make a glowing spot; put it in a tinder bundle and blow. Fire piston: a cylinder and plunger. Put char cloth in the plunger tip, drive it in hard and fast, then pull out at once — compressed air heats enough to make an ember. Chemical: some kits use potassium permanganate with glycerin, which ignites by itself after a delay. It is a strong oxidiser and can flare violently. Use only if you have practised with it and follow the kit's instructions.
Lay the kindling before you make the spark or ember. Leave gaps for air. Light from the upwind side so the wind pushes flame into the fuel.

s: fast start, hot flame — best for lighting and boiling
f: Teepee fast start, hot flame — best for lighting and boiling
t: Lean kindling over the tinder; leave a door on the upwind side to light it. Put the tinder bundle on a dry base. Lean pencil-lead and pencil-thick sticks around it in a cone; leave a door facing the wind. Add a looser outer layer of thumb-thick sticks. Light through the door. Add fuel to the outside as it burns; it collapses into coals.

s: stable, lots of coals — cooking and long burns
f: Log cabin stable, lots of coals — cooking and long burns
t: A crib of crossed sticks around a small teepee. Build a small teepee of tinder and kindling. Lay two thumb-to-wrist-thick sticks on either side, then two across them, like a cabin. Keep going, using slightly smaller sticks. Optionally lay a "roof" of kindling across the top. Light the teepee inside.

s: for wind — a log shelters the tinder
f: Lean-to fire lay for wind — a log shelters the tinder
t: The log goes on the windward side. Lay a large log (or rock that is dry) on the upwind side. Put the tinder against its downwind side. Lean kindling from the ground onto the log, over the tinder. Light from the end, keeping your body as an extra windbreak.

s: saves fuel; long, slow burn with no chopping
f: Star fire saves fuel; long, slow burn with no chopping
t: Top view. Only the tips burn; slide each log in as it shortens. Start a small fire. Lay 4–6 long logs with their ends meeting in the fire, like spokes. Push the logs in as the ends burn. Pull them out to cut the heat.

s: low visibility, strong draught, good in wind
f: Dakota fire hole low visibility, strong draught, good in wind
t: Cross-section. The air hole is on the upwind side. Dig a fire hole roughly 1 ft (30 cm) wide and deep. About a hand-span or two away, on the upwind side, dig a smaller air hole angled down to meet the bottom of the fire hole. Build the fire in the bottom of the fire hole. Air is drawn through the tunnel. Pots can sit across the top on green sticks. Don't dig in peat or roots Never dig a Dakota hole in peat, deep duff or a mat of roots: fire can smoulder underground and spread unseen. Use mineral soil only. Refill the holes and soak them when done.

s: warms your whole body when sleeping out
f: Long fire warms your whole body when sleeping out
t: Top view. Fire burns between two long logs. Lay two long logs side by side about a hand-span apart, as long as your body. Build the fire in the gap along its full length. Feed it to keep an even bed of coals. Sleep parallel to it with a clear, swept gap (about 3 ft / 1 m or more) — never downwind, and with nothing burnable between you and the fire. Someone stays awake to tend it, or you wake regularly. Pair it with a reflector wall behind the fire.

s: throws heat back toward you and your shelter
f: Reflector wall throws heat back toward you and your shelter
t: Logs stacked between stakes, on the far side of the fire from you. Drive two pairs of stakes about 1–2 ft (30–60 cm) behind where the fire will be. Stack green or damp logs between them to knee-to-waist height. A dry rock face also works, but heat it gently and don't sleep against it. Build the fire between the wall and your shelter. Heat that would escape is bounced toward you.

Three fires in a triangle (or a straight line), spaced well apart (roughly 75–100 ft / 25–30 m), is an internationally recognised distress signal. Three of anything = help. Daytime: smoke is seen better than flame. Pile green vegetation (fresh leaves, boughs, moss) on a hot fire for thick white smoke — best against dark forest. Over snow or pale ground, black smoke shows better: burn a little rubber or oil (spare tyre strips, oily rags). Stay upwind — that smoke is toxic. Night: bright flame. Keep signal fires built and ready (dry tinder protected under bark, green boughs nearby) so you can light them the moment you hear an aircraft. Use open ground or a clearing so smoke rises and the fire can't spread.

Cook over coals, not flame — steadier heat, less burning. A log cabin lay makes good coals. Boil water at a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m). See Water. Never put sealed cans or containers in a fire — they can burst.

Hang wet items on sticks beside the fire, not over it, and never leave them unattended. Turn them often. Synthetics melt and fleece can catch fire quickly; feel them often. Keep boots back — leather cracks and soles delaminate if too hot. Dry socks and gloves first, then base layers. Drying clothes on your body near a fire also works but takes time. Never bring a fire, stove or coals inside a tent or snow shelter to dry things. See carbon monoxide.

Look up, look down Widowmakers — dead trees and dead or hung-up branches — kill campers every year, often in wind at night. Never shelter under or within falling distance of them. Never shelter in a dry wash, gully or stream bed: flash floods can arrive from rain you can't see or hear. Avoid valley bottoms and hollows — cold air sinks and pools there at night, and they collect fog, frost and water. Avoid exposed ridgetops — wind and lightning. A flat bench partway up a slope is often warmest. Near materials and water, but not right beside water — a short walk away (roughly 200 ft / 60 m): drier, fewer insects, safer from rising water and animals coming to drink. Use natural windbreaks: boulders, thickets, the lee side of a ridge or a big fallen log (check it's stable). Drainage: a slight rise with firm, dry ground. Water must run away from your bed, not into it. Avoid avalanche and rockfall paths, ant nests, animal trails and lone tall trees. If you want to be found, stay near an open area where you can lay out signals and build signal fires.

s: no tools or tarp needed; warm without a fire
f: Debris hut no tools or tarp needed; warm without a fire
t: Side view. Ridgepole on a stump or forked prop; ribs leaning on it; then a deep pile of leaves and debris. Ridgepole: a sturdy pole about 1.5× your height. Rest one end on a stump, rock or forked prop about hip-to-waist high; the other end on the ground. Check the size: lie under it. You want just enough room to roll over — small is warm; your body heats the space. Ribs: lean sticks closely along both sides of the ridgepole, steep enough to shed rain. Leave a small entrance at the high end. Lattice: lay brushy twigs across the ribs so the debris doesn't fall through. Debris: pile dry leaves, needles, grass and ferns on top — at least 2–3 ft (60–90 cm) thick, more in cold or rain. It takes far more than you think. Top with branches to stop it blowing away. Bed: fill the inside with a thick layer of dry debris and compress it. You'll lie on and under debris — insulation underneath matters most. Door: keep the entrance small and facing away from the wind (leeward). Once inside, plug it with a pile of debris or a stuffed pack. No fire inside Never have a fire, stove or candle in or near a debris hut — it is a pile of dry fuel.

s: quick; best with a fire and reflector in front
f: Lean-to quick; best with a fire and reflector in front
t: Side view. Open side faces the fire; the roof takes the wind. Check the wind. Plan for the back of the roof to face into it. (Wind can shift at night — in valleys cold air often flows downhill.) Lash or wedge a ridgepole between two trees or on two forked uprights, about waist-to-chest high. Lean poles from the ridgepole to the ground on the windward side, fairly steep so rain runs off. Cover with boughs, bark or debris, starting at the bottom and overlapping upward like roof tiles. Make it thick. Build a thick bed of dry debris under the roof. Build a fire in front of the open side with a reflector wall beyond it. Keep a clear gap between bed and fire.

Snow is a good insulator: inside a well-built snow shelter it often stays near freezing even when it is far colder outside. They take hours and make you wet — work slowly to avoid sweating, and wear waterproof outer layers. Danger — suffocation & carbon monoxide Always keep a ventilation hole open and check it often, especially while snow is falling or drifting. Inner walls glaze over and seal as you breathe and warm the space. Never run a stove, heater, grill or generator inside a tent, snow shelter, vehicle or home: carbon monoxide kills. Even a candle burns oxygen and gives off some CO — only with the vent open, and never left lit while you sleep. Keep a digging tool inside with you in case of collapse or drifting at the entrance. Build away from avalanche slopes and their run-out zones.

s: works with any snow, even shallow or powdery
f: Quinzhee (snow mound) works with any snow, even shallow or powdery
t: Cross-section. Dig out until you reach the stick ends — that leaves walls about 1 ft (30 cm) thick. Pile snow into a mound about 6–7 ft (2 m) high and 8–10 ft (2.5–3 m) across. Mix and stir the snow as you pile it — it helps it set. Let it sinter (settle and harden) for 1–2 hours, longer in very cold, dry snow. Rest, eat and drink meanwhile — don't get sweaty. Push dozens of sticks about 1 ft (30 cm) long into the mound all over, pointing at the centre. These are depth gauges. Dig a low entrance on the downwind side. Tunnel in, then hollow out upward and outward. Stop digging wherever you reach the end of a stick: that leaves walls about 30 cm (1 ft) thick. Leave a raised sleeping platform above the entrance level. Cold air sinks into the low entrance trench, away from you. Smooth the ceiling into a dome so drips run down the walls instead of onto you. Push a fist-sized vent hole through the roof at an angle. Keep a stick in it and wiggle it clear regularly. Insulate the platform (pad, boughs, pack). Partly block the door with a pack or snow block — never airtight. Mark the outside with a pole or bright item.

s: fastest snow shelter in firm, deep snow
f: Snow trench fastest snow shelter in firm, deep snow
t: Mark a trench a little longer than you and about shoulder-width. Dig down about 3 ft (1 m) in firm snow, keeping walls straight. Cut blocks if the snow allows. Roof it: lean snow blocks together in an A shape, or lay branches, skis or a tarp across and cover with snow. Make the entrance at one end, lower than your bed, so cold air drains out of the sleeping area. Insulate the floor, open a vent, keep your digging tool inside.

s: under big conifers where snow is shallow by the trunk
f: Tree-well shelter under big conifers where snow is shallow by the trunk
t: Choose a large evergreen with low, dense branches. Check for dead branches and heavy snow loads above. Dig down beside the trunk into the well under the branches. Line the floor thickly with boughs; add boughs over gaps in the roof. Keep any fire outside and away from the branches — heat melts the snow above, which can dump onto you or the fire. Tree wells can trap you Deep, loose snow around trees can collapse inward. People who fall in head-first can suffocate. Approach carefully, and never dig a deep well alone in loose powder.

Run a taut ridgeline between two trees (use a bowline at one end and a taut-line hitch or trucker's hitch at the other). Point the lowest, most closed side into the wind. Pitch the tarp tight so rain runs off. Basic tarp shapes (accent arrows = wind). Set-up Best when Notes A-frame Rain, wind from changing directions Simple and stable. Pitch low and close the ends with gear or brush in bad weather. Lean-to Mild weather with a fire in front Lots of open space and heat from the fire. Poor if wind or rain swings round. Plough point (diamond) Steady wind from one direction; solo One corner high on a tree or pole, opposite corner staked into the wind. Quick, needs one anchor. Wedge / tarp tent Strong wind and driving rain Low back into the wind, sides staked to the ground. Warmest tarp shape, least room. C-fly Wet ground; with a fire in front A lean-to whose lower part folds back under you as a groundsheet — roof, back wall and floor from one tarp.

Insulate underneath first. Pad, thick boughs, leaves, your pack under your legs. You lose heat into the ground far faster than into the air. Layers: a wicking base (wool or synthetic — cotton stays wet and cold), an insulating middle, a wind- and waterproof shell. Add and remove layers to stay just cool, not sweaty. Vent before you sweat. Open zips and remove a layer before hard work. Sweat freezes and soaks insulation. Cover head, neck, hands and feet. Change into dry socks and base layer for sleeping; keep one dry set just for that. Eat and drink before sleeping. A snack with fat and carbs fuels heat through the night. Dehydration makes you colder. Empty your bladder before settling in. Hot water bottle: fill a leak-proof bottle made for hot liquids with hot water, close it tightly, check for leaks, wrap it in a sock or cloth and put it in your sleeping bag by your core or thighs. Never against bare skin — it can burn. Share heat: sleep close together; put the coldest person in the middle. Vapour barrier (deep cold only): a plastic bag or liner inside your insulation, over a thin base layer, stops body moisture soaking your bag on multi-day trips well below freezing. It feels clammy — use it briefly and only when it's very cold. Spot and treat hypothermia: see First aid.

Five knots cover most camp jobs. In the diagrams the coloured rope is the working end (the end you move) and the plain rope is the standing part (the rest of the rope). A gap in a line means that strand passes underneath. Not for life support without training Climbing, rescue, lowering people or anything where a failure could kill needs proper instruction, rated rope and hardware. Practise every knot until you can tie it with your eyes closed — and with cold hands.

s: a fixed loop that won't slip or jam
t: Use it for: a loop round a tree or post (one end of a ridgeline), a loop to hang or haul things. Easy to untie even after a heavy load. 1: make the hole with the end side on top. 2: up through the hole, round behind the standing part, back down the hole. Leave enough rope for the loop size you want. Make a small loop (the "hole") in the standing part, with the part leading to the working end lying on top. "The rabbit comes up out of the hole": pass the working end up through the hole from underneath. "Round the tree": take it round behind the standing part. "Back down the hole": pass it back down through the hole, alongside where it came up. Hold the tail and the loop side together and pull the standing part to tighten. Leave a long tail — at least a hand-width. Check: the tail ends up inside the big loop; a neat collar wraps the standing part; the small loop grips both strands. If the tail is outside the loop or it pulls into a slip knot, untie and retie. Limitations A bowline can shake loose when it isn't loaded (flapping guy lines, stiff or slippery rope), and it can't be tied or untied under load. For anything important, back it up: tie a stopper knot (double overhand) with the tail around the loop leg next to it, or use a Yosemite finish (tail round that loop leg and back up through the collar beside the standing part).

s: adjustable tension for guy lines and ridgelines
t: Use it for: tent and tarp guy lines, a ridgeline end. Slide it to tighten or loosen; it grips under load. Two turns inside the loop (toward the stake), one turn outside tucked under itself. Gaps show where the cord passes behind the standing part. Pass the working end around the stake, peg or tree and back toward the load, alongside the standing part. Wrap it twice around the standing part, working back toward the stake — these two turns are inside the loop. Bring the end back out past those turns, to the side away from the stake (outside the loop). Make one more turn around the standing part in the same direction, and tuck the end under itself (a half hitch). Pull snug. Slide the knot along the standing part to set the tension. Let go: it should hold. Check: two turns between the outside hitch and the stake, one hitch outside, all turns going the same way round. It should slide only when you push the knot itself. Limitations Slips on slippery, stiff, very thin or icy cord — add a third inside turn. Re-check tension after rain or a temperature change.

s: quick attachment to a post, pole or tree
t: Use it for: tying a line to a pole or stake quickly, starting and finishing lashings, adjusting a line midway along a rope. Front of a post. Dashed lines run behind the post. The rider (diagonal) crosses over both rope ends. Pass the working end around the post. Cross over the standing part — this diagonal is the rider — and go around the post a second time, in the same direction. Tuck the end under the rider, so it comes out between the two turns. Pull both ends tight. Check: from the front, one diagonal rider with both ends coming out from under it, in opposite directions. From the back, two neat parallel turns. Limitations A clove hitch can slip or roll on its own — when the pull comes from the side, the pole turns, or the load keeps shifting. Secure it with two half hitches of the tail around the standing part.

s: bandages, bundles, tying the two ends of one cord
t: Use it for: tying off a bandage or sling, closing a bundle or bag — the two ends of the same cord around something. Lies flat; easy to untie. Loose square knot: two interlocked loops; both short ends on the same side. Right over left and tuck under (like starting to tie a shoe). Left over right and tuck under. Pull both ends evenly. Each end lies beside its own standing part. Check: it lies flat and symmetric, with both short ends on the same side. If you did right-over-left twice you get a granny knot: it looks twisted, the ends stick out crosswise, and it slips or jams — retie it. Not for joining ropes Never use a square knot to join two ropes — especially of different size or material — or for any load that matters. It can capsize and pull apart. To join two ropes use a sheet bend (below).

s: friction hitch that grips when loaded and slides when not
t: Use it for: a movable attachment point on a ridgeline (e.g. tensioning a tarp), a grip to pull on a rope, a hauling or backup grab. You need a closed loop of cord thinner than the main rope — typically 5–7 mm cord on 10–11 mm rope. Seen from the side the legs come out: three wraps make six neat coils. Hold the cord loop behind the main rope. Pass the far end of the loop over the rope and through itself (a girth hitch), but don't tighten. Keep wrapping through the inside of the loop, each wrap beside the last, for 3 wraps in total. Dress it: wraps neat and parallel with no crossovers, a straight bridge on one side, legs coming out of the middle. Pull the legs to test: it should grip. To move it, unload it and push the knot body, not the legs. Check: six tidy coils, legs centred, grips firmly when you hang on it. If it slips, add a wrap or use thinner cord; if it won't slide, take a wrap off. Limitations Grips poorly on icy, wet, muddy or slick rope, and with cord too close to the main rope's thickness. A sudden shock can make it slip and melt the cord. Using a prusik to hold a person (climbing, ascending, rescue) requires training and rated gear.

s: sheet bend, trucker's hitch, two half hitches, figure-eight stopper
t: Sheet bend — joins two ropes, even of different thickness. Make a U-shaped bight in the thicker rope. Pass the thinner end up through the bight, around behind both legs of the bight, then tuck it under itself (not under the bight). Both short ends should end up on the same side. Go around twice (double sheet bend) for slippery or very unequal ropes. Leave long tails. Trucker's hitch — high tension. Tie a fixed loop partway along the standing part (e.g. a figure-eight on a bight). Take the end round the anchor, back up through that loop, and pull down — it multiplies your pull (less in practice, because of friction). Pinch it and finish with two half hitches. Friction wears the rope where it runs through the loop. Two half hitches — tie a rope end to a ring, post or tree. Pass the end around the object, then around the standing part and through (one half hitch); repeat in the same direction. Start with a full extra turn around the object (round turn and two half hitches) to take a heavy load. Figure-eight stopper — stops a rope end pulling through. Make a loop near the end, take the end around behind the standing part, then down through the loop. It looks like an 8, holds well and unties easily.

Carbon monoxide (CO) Never run a stove, heater, grill or generator inside a tent, snow shelter, vehicle or home: carbon monoxide kills. You can't see or smell it. A generator must be at least 20 ft (6 m) from doors and windows, exhaust pointed away. Warning signs: headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion, sleepiness — often several people at once. Get everyone into fresh air immediately and get medical help. Stuck in a vehicle in snow? Keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow. Wildfire Most wildfires are started by people. Clear the site, keep fires small, never leave one unattended, and put it out cold. Skip fire entirely in high wind or very dry conditions. If a fire gets away or a wildfire approaches: leave early. Fire moves fastest uphill and downwind — don't try to outrun it uphill. Head for natural firebreaks: wide rocky ground, water, roads or already-burned ground. Avoid narrow canyons and gullies, which act like chimneys. Hypothermia from wet clothing Wet clothes plus wind can make you dangerously cold even well above freezing. Watch for shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech, poor decisions — shivering that stops is a bad sign. Handle the person gently. Get them out of wind and wet, remove wet clothing, insulate them from the ground, and warm the core (armpits, chest, groin). Warm sweet drinks only if fully alert and able to swallow. No alcohol. Don't rub limbs. More in First aid. Back to top

Read this first This is not a substitute for professional training or medical care. If there is any way to reach help, call emergency services first, then use this page while you wait. 911 (US)112 (EU / Portugal) 112 works across the EU and on most mobile phones worldwide. Many phones can call 112/911 without a SIM or on another carrier's network — some countries block this, so try anyway. No voice signal? Text 911 where available (US); texts often get through when calls fail. Climb higher for signal. Newer phones and satellite messengers/PLBs can send SOS via satellite with no cell signal. Learn how yours works before you need it. Get the person to real medical help as soon as it is safely possible. Get trained: Stop the Bleed, CPR/AED, and a Wilderness First Aid course. Practise with your own kit. Field steps for the first minutes and hours after an injury or illness, when help is far away. Aligned with Red Cross, American Heart Association, Stop the Bleed and Wilderness Medical Society guidance. Short, conservative, step-numbered.

Scene safe? Traffic, fire, water, electricity, falling rock, the animal. Don't become a second casualty. Gloves (or a plastic bag) on if you have them. Check responsiveness and breathing. Tap the shoulders, shout "Are you OK?" Look at the chest for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing. Call for help. 911 / 112 on speaker. Send someone for an AED and a first-aid kit. Give your location first. Stop major bleeding. Blood spurting, pooling or soaking through clothing kills in minutes: press hard, pack, or apply a tourniquet. How → Not breathing normally? Start CPR — push hard and fast in the centre of the chest. How → Breathing but unresponsive? Put them in the recovery position to keep the airway clear. Keep them warm and still (prevent shock): insulate from the ground, cover, reassure, re-check breathing every few minutes. Shock → Tell the dispatcher: where you are (coordinates from the Map), what happened, how many people are hurt, how they are now, and what you have done.

Life-threatening bleeding: blood spurting or flowing steadily, pooling on the ground, soaking through clothing or bandages, a partly or fully amputated limb, or a person getting pale, confused or faint.
k: bleed bleeding stop the bleed blood loss hemorrhage

t: Protect yourself: gloves or a plastic bag over your hand if possible — but don't delay. Expose the wound. Cut or tear clothing away so you can see where the blood is coming from. Put a dressing or clean cloth on the wound and press hard with both hands, body weight over straight arms. If you have nothing, use your hand. Don't lift to peek. If blood soaks through, leave the first layer and add more on top — or, for a deep wound, pack it (below). Keep pressing until the bleeding stops and ideally until help takes over. Then wrap a firm pressure bandage over the dressing. Arm or leg still bleeding heavily despite hard pressure? Tourniquet.

h: 2. Wound packing (deep wounds and junctional wounds)
f: 2. Wound packing (deep wounds and junctional wounds)
t: Use for deep wounds, and for the neck, armpit and groin (junctional areas) where a tourniquet cannot work — pack and press there instead. Open the wound enough to find where the blood is coming from. Push gauze (hemostatic gauze is best, plain gauze or clean cloth will do) right onto the bleeding point with your fingers. Keep feeding it in, packing tightly, until the wound cavity is completely full and packing stands slightly proud of the skin. Press hard with both hands on top of the packing. Hold without letting go — hemostatic gauze needs at least the time on its packet (typically 3 minutes); plain gauze longer. Keep holding if help is coming. Wrap a pressure bandage tightly over the packing (not around the neck — on the neck, keep pressing by hand). Neck wounds Never wrap anything tightly around the neck. Pack and press by hand, keep the airway clear, and evacuate urgently.

A commercial windlass tourniquet (CAT, SOF-T Wide or similar) is strongly preferred. Buy from a reputable supplier — counterfeits break. Practise with it. "Above" the wound means between the wound and the body. The dashed band near the hip shows "high and tight" placement when you can't see where the bleeding is. Place the band 2–3 in (5–7 cm) above the wound — between the wound and the body — not on a joint. If the wound is just below a knee or elbow, go above the joint. If you can't tell where the wound is, or there are several: "high and tight" on the limb. Pull the strap as tight as you can and fasten it. Empty bulky pockets under it if possible. Twist the windlass until the bleeding stops. It will hurt badly — that is expected. Tell them so. Lock the windlass in its clip so it can't unwind. Write the time on the patient (forehead: "TK 14:35") or on the tourniquet tag. Still bleeding after it is fully tightened? Put a second tourniquet just above the first (closer to the body) and tighten it. Leave it uncovered and visible. Get to emergency care as fast as possible. Never loosen a tourniquet Once applied, do not loosen or remove it — leave that to a hospital. Loosening can restart fatal bleeding. A tourniquet on a limb means evacuate now.
k: tourniquet stop bleeding arm leg limb

t: Improvised tourniquets often fail. Hard direct pressure and packing are better than a bad improvised tourniquet. Use one only if pressure isn't controlling limb bleeding, or you must free your hands for other casualties. Band: at least 1.5 in (4 cm) wide — folded triangular bandage, strip of strong cloth. Tie it around the limb (placement as above) with a half-knot. Windlass: a strong stick or rod. Lay it on the half-knot and tie a full knot over it. Twist until the bleeding stops. Tie or tape the windlass down so it can't unwind. Write the time. Never use Wire, cord, string, shoelaces, zip ties or thin rope. They cut into the limb and don't compress the artery.

Sit up and lean forward (not back — swallowed blood causes vomiting). Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly, just below the bony bridge. Breathe through the mouth; spit out blood. Hold continuously for 10–15 minutes without checking. Repeat once if needed. Get medical help if it hasn't stopped after about 20 minutes of good pressure, follows a head injury, is very heavy, or the person takes blood thinners.

Infection, not the cut itself, is the main danger of a wound in the field. The best tool is a lot of clean water under pressure. Stop the bleeding first. Wash your hands; gloves on. Irrigate: flush the wound with lots of clean water — ideally drinkable (disinfected) water, a litre (quart) or more for a dirty wound. Use pressure: an irrigation syringe, or a clean plastic bag or bottle with a pinhole, squeezed hard, held close to the wound. See Water for disinfecting. Remove debris you can see with clean tweezers (boil or wipe with alcohol first). Irrigate again. Clean the skin around the wound with soap and water. Don't pour alcohol, hydrogen peroxide or strong iodine into the wound — they damage tissue. Minor, clean wounds: thin layer of antibiotic ointment or petroleum jelly, then a non-stick sterile dressing. Change the dressing daily, or when wet or dirty. Look at the wound each time. Don't close these wounds in the field Dirty wounds, animal or human bites, punctures, and wounds you couldn't clean well. Closing traps bacteria. Irrigate, pack loosely with a moist clean dressing, cover, and get to care. Only small, clean, well-irrigated cuts may be held together with wound-closure strips. Infection — evacuate Increasing pain, swelling and warmth; spreading redness; red streaks running up the limb; pus; fever or chills. These need antibiotics. Draw a pen line around the edge of the redness with the time to see if it spreads. Tetanus: for dirty wounds, punctures and bites, a …

t: Wash the bite or scratch with soap and running water for 15 minutes. This greatly lowers rabies risk. Irrigate, cover, don't close it. Seek post-exposure treatment urgently after any bite or scratch from a bat, fox, raccoon, skunk, a wild mammal behaving oddly, or a dog/cat of unknown health. Bat contact counts even if you can't see a bite. Rabies Once symptoms start, rabies is almost always fatal. Treatment after the bite but before symptoms works. Don't wait to see if you get sick — go.

Stop the burning. Move away from the source. Clothes on fire: stop, drop, roll; smother with a blanket. Cool with cool running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible. Cool the burn, not the whole person — keep them warm otherwise. Remove rings, watches and clothing near the burn before swelling starts — unless stuck to the skin. Cover loosely with cling film (lay strips on, don't wrap tightly) or a clean non-fluffy dressing. A clean plastic bag works for a hand. Don't pop blisters. Give pain relief per label (see Medicines). No ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or creams on a fresh burn. Don't pull off anything stuck to the burn. Get medical care for Large burns (bigger than the person's hand), deep burns (white, leathery, charred or painless), burns to the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, any airway burn (soot around mouth or nose, singed nose hairs, hoarse voice, coughing — the airway can swell shut), electrical and chemical burns, and burns on children or the elderly.
k: burn burns scald

t: Protect yourself — gloves. Brush off dry chemical first, then remove contaminated clothing and jewellery. Flush with lots of running water for at least 20 minutes. Eyes: hold the lids open, flush from the inner corner outward, away from the other eye. Get medical care. Keep the container or label.

Don't touch the person while they are still in contact with the power. Switch off at the source if you safely can. Downed or high-voltage lines: stay well back — at least 18 m (about 60 ft) — and wait for the power company or emergency services. Once safe: check breathing; be ready for CPR — electricity can stop the heart. Cool and cover burns. Always get medical care — internal damage is far worse than the skin shows, and heart-rhythm problems can follow.
Possible fracture: deformity, swelling and bruising, sharp pain at one spot, can't use or bear weight, grating, or bone visible in a wound. If in doubt, treat it as broken.

Control bleeding and cover any wound. Check CSM beyond the injury — Circulation (warm, pink, pulse), Sensation (can feel your touch), Movement (can wiggle fingers/toes). Note it. Support the limb in the position found. Immobilise the joint above and the joint below a broken bone (for a joint injury: the bones above and below). Pad well — bony points, hollows, and between legs or arm and body. Tie it on firmly, not tight. Knots on the splint, not over the injury. Re-check CSM after splinting and every 15–30 minutes. Numbness, tingling, pale/blue or cold fingers or toes: loosen the ties. Elevate if possible; wrapped cold pack 20 minutes at a time; pain relief per label. Remote, no circulation If the hand or foot beyond a broken long bone is cold, pale or blue and pulseless, and help is hours away, a trained person may gently straighten an angled shaft fracture with steady pull in line with the limb to restore blood flow (WMS). Stop if pain sharply increases or you meet resistance. Never on joints or the spine. Don't try to put dislocations back unless trained.

SAM splint: mould it on your own uninjured limb first, then apply. A curve along its length makes it rigid. Sticks, trekking poles, tent poles — padded, one each side. Rolled foam sleeping pad — excellent for legs and arms. Rolled newspaper or magazine for a forearm or wrist; a pillow or jacket wrapped around an ankle. Buddy splinting: tape a finger or toe to its neighbour with padding between; tie legs together with padding between knees and ankles. Ties: triangular bandages, strips of cloth, belts, tape — wide is better than narrow.

h: Sling and swathe (arm, wrist, collarbone, shoulder)
f: Sling and swathe (arm, wrist, collarbone, shoulder)
t: Sling: support the forearm across the chest, hand slightly higher than the elbow, with a triangular bandage or jacket tied around the neck (pad the knot). Swathe: a second wide band around the body and over the arm to bind the arm to the chest. Check fingers for circulation and feeling.

Control bleeding with pressure around the bone end, not on it. Rinse off gross dirt, then cover with a sterile or clean moist dressing. Don't push the bone back in. Splint as found. Evacuate — high risk of serious infection. Treat for shock. Thigh or pelvis A broken thigh bone or pelvis can bleed internally enough to kill. Don't rock the pelvis to test it. Treat for shock, keep warm, evacuate urgently.

Suspect it after falls from height, diving, vehicle crashes, a heavy blow to the head, or if there is neck/back pain, numbness, tingling or weakness, or the person is confused or intoxicated. Don't move them unless they are in danger (fire, water, rockfall, avalanche) or you must to open the airway or do CPR. Manual stabilisation: kneel at the head, hold it with both hands in line with the body. Tell them not to move. Insulate from the ground and keep warm — tuck padding in with minimal movement. If you must move them: log-roll with several helpers, keeping head, neck and body in one line, on the count of the person at the head. Vomiting or you must leave them: roll onto their side keeping the spine aligned — the airway comes first.

Rest the joint. Ice (or cold water / cold pack) wrapped in cloth, 20 minutes at a time. Never directly on skin; skip it if they're getting cold. Compression with an elastic bandage — snug, not tight; check toes/fingers. Elevation above the heart when resting. Treat as a fracture and splint if they can't take 4 steps, or there is bone tenderness or deformity.

Stage Signs Mild Shivering, cold pale skin, the "umbles": stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles. Poor judgement. Moderate Violent then weakening shivering, worsening confusion, drowsiness, slurred speech, clumsiness, odd behaviour (may even undress). Severe Shivering stops. Barely responsive or unresponsive. Slow, weak breathing and pulse — may look dead. Handle gently, especially in moderate/severe cases — rough handling can trigger cardiac arrest. Keep severe cases lying flat; don't let them walk. Get out of wind and wet. Shelter, windbreak, tarp. Insulate from the ground — pads, packs, branches, rope coils. Remove wet clothing (cut it off to avoid moving them much) and replace with dry layers. If you can't, put a plastic layer around them inside the insulation. Hypothermia wrap ("burrito") — see diagram. Cover the head and neck; leave the face open. Warm the core: warm-water bottles or heat packs wrapped in cloth to the armpits, chest and groin (never directly on skin — burns). Skin-to-skin with a warm person also works. Warm sweet drinks only if fully alert and able to swallow. High-energy food for mild cases. No alcohol. Don't rub or massage limbs. No hot bath or shower for moderate/severe cases. Evacuate moderate and severe hypothermia — gently, lying flat. Hypothermia wrap, end-on view. Build it on the ground layer by layer, then fold the tarp around the whole bundle. Leave the face uncovered. Severe hypothermia Check breathing for longer than usual — up to a full …
