t: Frostnip: numb, pale skin that recovers fully with warming. Frostbite: white or grey waxy skin; deep frostbite is hard and wooden with no feeling. Treat hypothermia first if present. Get out of the cold; remove rings and tight items. Don't rub it — not with snow, not with hands. It destroys tissue. Rewarm only if there is no risk of it refreezing. Thaw-then-refreeze causes far worse damage. If you must walk out on frozen feet, keep them frozen — never walk on thawed feet. Rewarm in warm water, 37–39 °C (99–102 °F) — test with a thermometer or an unaffected elbow. Keep it at that temperature until the skin is soft and colour and feeling return (often around 30 minutes). It hurts: give pain relief (ibuprofen per label, if safe for them). No direct heat — fire, stove, heater, engine. Numb skin burns without feeling it. Leave blisters intact. Loose, dry, padded dressings, with padding between fingers and toes. Elevate. Protect from cold and pressure. Get medical care for anything beyond frostnip.

Heat exhaustion Heat stroke — EMERGENCY Mind Alert; maybe dizzy, headache, irritable Confused, odd behaviour, slurred speech, seizure, collapse — the key sign Skin Sweaty, pale, clammy Hot; may be dry or still sweating Body Heavy sweating, thirst, cramps, nausea, weakness, fast pulse Very high body temperature, fast pulse and breathing, vomiting Do Shade, lie down, raise legs, loosen clothing, wet skin and fan, sip water or electrolyte drink. Should improve within 30 minutes — if not, treat as heat stroke. Call 911/112. Cool immediately and aggressively: cold-water immersion up to the neck is best. Otherwise soak with water and fan constantly; cold wet cloths or ice packs on neck, armpits, groin, swapped often. Nothing to drink unless fully alert. Recovery position if unresponsive. Hot + confused = heat stroke Don't wait for transport to start cooling. Every minute of high body temperature damages the brain and organs. Keep cooling until they are clearly improving.

1 minute Cold shock. Gasping and fast breathing. Keep your head up, don't thrash, lean back and float, and get your breathing under control. Most cold-water deaths happen here, from inhaling water. 10 minutes Useful movement. Hands and arms are failing. Self-rescue now: get out, or onto something, or tie yourself to something that keeps your face out of the water. 1 hour Before unconsciousness from hypothermia (roughly — varies). With a lifejacket, keep still: knees to chest (HELP position), or huddle together. Rescuers: reach or throw, don't go. Use a pole, rope, branch or anything that floats. Lie flat on ice. After rescue: handle gently, keep horizontal, treat for hypothermia. Anyone who inhaled water needs medical checks even if they seem fine.

Not enough blood flow to the organs. Causes: bleeding (seen or internal), burns, severe allergic reaction, dehydration, infection, heart problems. It gets worse without treatment. Signs: pale or grey, cold and clammy skin; fast, weak pulse; fast shallow breathing; anxious or restless, then confused or drowsy; thirst; nausea; weakness; finally unresponsive. Call 911/112 / start evacuation planning now. Treat the cause: stop bleeding; epinephrine for anaphylaxis; cool burns. Lay them flat on their back. If breathing is difficult, let them sit in the most comfortable position. If vomiting or unresponsive, recovery position. Legs: you may raise them about 30 cm (12 in) only if there is no injury to the legs, hips, pelvis, neck or back and it doesn't cause pain. If unsure, leave them flat. Keep warm: insulate from the ground and cover. Prevent heat loss, but don't overheat. Nothing by mouth if they may need surgery or are not fully alert. (If help is many hours or days away and they are fully alert with no belly injury, small sips of water are reasonable.) Reassure, loosen tight clothing, check breathing and responsiveness every few minutes. Be ready to start CPR. Evacuate. Shock needs hospital care.

Unresponsive and not breathing normally (or only gasping) = start CPR. Compressions keep blood moving to the brain. Scene safe. Tap and shout. Check breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Call 911/112 on speaker and get an AED. Alone with a phone: call first, then start — the dispatcher will coach you. Person on their back on a firm surface. Kneel beside the chest. Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top, fingers laced. Arms straight, shoulders over hands. Push hard and fast: 100–120 per minute, at least 2 in (5 cm) but not more than 2.4 in (6 cm) deep. Let the chest fully recoil each time. Minimise pauses. Trained and willing: after 30 compressions, tilt the head back, lift the chin, pinch the nose and give 2 breaths (about 1 second each, just enough to make the chest rise). 30 compressions : 2 breaths. Otherwise: hands-only CPR — continuous compressions. AED as soon as available: switch it on and follow its voice. Pads on bare, dry chest. Stand clear when it analyses and shocks. Restart compressions immediately after. Don't stop until they breathe normally or move, the AED tells you to, trained help takes over, you are exhausted, or the scene becomes unsafe. Swap compressors about every 2 minutes. Drowning The problem is lack of oxygen. If trained, start with rescue breaths (European guidance: 5 initial breaths), then continue 30:2. Untrained: compressions are still far better than nothing.
k: cpr not breathing cardiac arrest heart chest compressions

s: Differences from adult CPR
f: Children and infants Differences from adult CPR
t: Child (1 year to puberty): one or two hands, compress about 1/3 of the chest depth (about 2 in / 5 cm), same rate. Rescue breaths matter more in children — give them if you can. Infant (under 1 year): centre of the chest just below the nipple line, with two thumbs (hands encircling the chest) or two fingers; depth about 1/3 of the chest (about 1.5 in / 4 cm). Cover mouth and nose with your mouth for gentle puffs. Alone with no phone: give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call for help. AED: use child pads if the child is under 8 and they are available; otherwise adult pads (front and back if they would touch).

For someone unresponsive but breathing normally. Keeps the airway open and lets vomit drain. Kneel beside them. Place the arm nearest you at a right angle to the body, elbow bent, palm up. Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek. With your other hand, pull the far knee up so the foot is flat on the ground. Pull on the far knee to roll them toward you onto their side. Adjust the top leg so hip and knee are bent at right angles — this stops them rolling forward. Tilt the head back gently and lift the chin to keep the airway open; mouth angled downward. Keep checking breathing. If it stops, roll them onto their back and start CPR. Pregnant: on the left side.
Mild: can cough forcefully and speak — encourage coughing, stay with them, don't hit them. Severe: can't speak, cough or breathe; may clutch the throat; lips turning blue — act now.
k: choking choke heimlich

t: Ask "Are you choking?" Get someone to call 911/112. Stand behind and slightly to the side. Support the chest with one hand and lean them well forward. 5 back blows: firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Check after each. 5 abdominal thrusts: arms around the waist, fist (thumb side in) just above the belly button, well below the breastbone. Grab the fist with your other hand and pull sharply in and up. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or they become unresponsive. Unresponsive: lower them to the ground, call 911/112, start CPR. Each time you open the airway, look in the mouth and remove any object you can see. No blind finger sweeps. Anyone who received abdominal thrusts must be checked by a doctor afterwards. Pregnant or large person If you can't get around the waist, or in late pregnancy: give chest thrusts instead — hands on the lower half of the breastbone, pull sharply straight back.

Call 911/112 even if you can't speak — leave the line open. Give yourself abdominal thrusts with your fist, or throw your upper belly hard against the back of a chair, a table edge or a railing. Repeat until it comes out.

Sit or kneel. Lay the baby face down along your forearm, head lower than the chest, supporting the jaw with your hand (don't cover the mouth or press the throat). Rest your arm on your thigh. Up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Turn the baby face up on your other forearm, supporting the head, head lower than chest. Up to 5 chest thrusts: two fingers in the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, push down sharply about 1/3 of the chest depth. Repeat until the object is out or the baby becomes unresponsive — then start infant CPR and call 911/112. Infants Never give abdominal thrusts to an infant. Never do blind finger sweeps. Don't hold a baby upside down by the legs.

s: Epinephrine first, always evacuate
f: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) Epinephrine first, always evacuate
t: Signs (usually within minutes): swelling of lips, tongue, face or throat; hoarse voice; trouble breathing or wheezing; hives spreading over the body; vomiting; dizziness or collapse — after a sting, food or medicine. Call 911/112. Use their epinephrine auto-injector immediately into the outer mid-thigh — through clothing if needed. Hold it in place for the time printed on the device. Position: sitting up if breathing is hard; lying flat with legs raised if faint or dizzy; recovery position if unresponsive and breathing. Don't let them stand or walk suddenly — they can collapse. No improvement after 5–15 minutes and a second injector is available? Give it (other thigh). Antihistamine tablets help itching and hives only — they do not treat anaphylaxis. Never delay epinephrine for them. Always evacuate, even if they recover — symptoms can return hours later. CPR if they stop breathing normally. An expired auto-injector is better than none in an emergency — but replace them before expiry.

s: Reliever inhaler, upright, calm
f: Asthma attack Reliever inhaler, upright, calm
t: Sit them upright, leaning slightly forward. Stay calm; loosen tight clothing. Help them use their own reliever inhaler (usually blue; salbutamol/albuterol), with a spacer if they have one. Follow their written asthma plan if they have one. UK guidance: 1 puff every 30–60 seconds, up to 10 puffs. Worse at any point, or not better after 10 puffs: call 911/112. If help hasn't come within 10 minutes, repeat. Emergency signs: can't speak full sentences, blue or grey lips, exhaustion, drowsiness or confusion.

s: Keep still, immobilise, evacuate
t: Move away from the snake. Don't try to catch or kill it; a photo from a safe distance is enough. Keep the person calm and still, lying down. Movement spreads venom — carry them out if you can. Call 911/112 and get to hospital. Antivenom is the only real treatment. Remove rings, watches, bracelets and tight clothing or boots from the bitten limb before it swells. Immobilise the limb with a splint, roughly at heart level. Mark the edge of the swelling with a pen and write the time. Repeat every 15–30 minutes. Wash gently with soap and water and cover loosely. For pain, acetaminophen/paracetamol — not ibuprofen or aspirin. No cutting, no sucking (by mouth or pump), no tourniquet, no ice, no electric shock, no alcohol. Pressure bandages Pressure-immobilisation (tight wrapping of the whole limb) is for some Australian and other elapid bites only. In North America and Europe most dangerous bites are from vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, European vipers and adders): immobilise without tight pressure.
k: snake bite snakebite viper rattlesnake venom

s: Tweezers close to the skin, steady pull
f: Tick removal Tweezers close to the skin, steady pull
t: Use fine-tipped tweezers. Grip the tick as close to the skin as possible. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. Don't twist, jerk or squeeze the body. Mouthparts left behind: remove with tweezers if easy; otherwise leave them and let the skin heal. Clean the bite and your hands with soap and water or alcohol. Seal the tick in tape or a bag; note the date. No burning, nail polish, petroleum jelly or other smothering — they delay removal. Watch for 3–30 days: an expanding rash (sometimes a "bull's-eye"), fever, chills, aches, fatigue. See a doctor and mention the tick bite.

s: Remove fast, cool, watch for anaphylaxis
f: Bee and wasp stings Remove fast, cool, watch for anaphylaxis
t: Bee stinger left in the skin: remove it quickly — scrape or pull; speed matters more than method. Wash; cold pack or cold water 10–20 minutes; elevate. Itch and swelling: antihistamine or hydrocortisone cream; pain relief per label. Any sign of anaphylaxis (face/throat swelling, breathing trouble, collapse): epinephrine and 911/112. Many stings, or a sting inside the mouth or throat: get medical help.

s: Oral rehydration solution recipe
f: Diarrhoea, vomiting & dehydration Oral rehydration solution recipe
t: Dehydration is the danger. Replace water and salts. Home oral rehydration solution (WHO-style) 1 litre clean water (boiled and cooled, or disinfected) + 6 level teaspoons sugar + 1/2 level teaspoon salt. Stir until dissolved. Make fresh daily. Commercial ORS packets are better if you have them. Sip small amounts often — a few mouthfuls every few minutes, even if vomiting. Keep eating simple food when able. Keep breastfeeding infants. Wash hands; disinfect water (see Water). Don't make it stronger Too much salt is dangerous, especially for children. Measure level teaspoons exactly. Get medical help for: blood or black stool, high fever, severe belly pain, very little or dark urine, dizziness on standing, sunken eyes, confusion or drowsiness, can't keep fluids down, lasting more than 2–3 days, or any infant, elderly or frail person.

s: Evacuate urgently if any are present
f: Head injury red flags Evacuate urgently if any are present
t: Any loss of consciousness, or drowsiness that is getting worse Confusion, unusual behaviour, memory loss Repeated vomiting; worsening headache Seizure Unequal pupils, slurred speech, weakness or numbness on one side Clear fluid or blood from the ears or nose; bruising behind the ears or around both eyes On blood thinners Suspect a neck injury with any significant head injury. Don't leave the person alone for 24 hours. No more activity that day, even if they "feel fine".

s: Flush, don't rub, protect
f: Eye injuries Flush, don't rub, protect
t: Grit or speck: don't rub. Blink; flush with clean water from the inner corner outward; pull the upper lid down over the lower lid. Chemical: flush with running water for at least 20 minutes, lids held open. Get care. Object stuck in the eye, or something hit it at speed (hammering, grinding): don't remove it or press on the eye. Cover loosely with a paper cup or padded ring and evacuate. Blow to the eye: cold pack without pressure. Get care if vision changes, there's blood in the front of the eye, or pain persists. Snow blindness (UV burn, gritty painful eyes): rest in the dark, cool compresses; usually heals in 1–2 days. Prevent with sunglasses or slit goggles.

s: Treat hot spots early
t: Hot spot (rubbing, warm, red): stop and cover it with smooth tape or moleskin now. Small intact blister: leave it intact; protect it with a "doughnut" of moleskin around it. Large, tense blister likely to burst: clean it, drain at the edge with a sterile needle (boiled or alcohol-wiped), leave the roof on, cover with a dressing. Torn blister: clean gently, cover, watch for infection. People with diabetes or poor circulation: don't drain — protect and get care.

Follow the package label — adult maximums only Doses below are adult limits. Children: only children's products, dosed by weight per the label. Ask about allergies first. Check for interactions (especially blood thinners, other painkillers, alcohol, sedatives) and for combination products containing the same drug. Pregnant or breastfeeding, kidney or liver disease, stomach ulcers, heart disease: check with a clinician or pharmacist first. Check expiry dates. Keep the leaflets. Medicine For Adult use Avoid / cautions Acetaminophen / paracetamol Pain, fever Dose per label (strengths differ). No more than 3,000 mg/day without doctor advice (label max 4,000 mg). Liver damage in overdose, often with no early symptoms — get help at once if too much was taken. Liver disease or regular alcohol use: ask first. Many cold/flu and "PM" products contain it — count all sources. Ibuprofen Pain, fever, swelling (sprains) 200–400 mg every 4–6 h, with food. Max 1,200 mg/day unless a doctor directs. Stomach bleeding, kidney risk — avoid when dehydrated. Not with ulcers, kidney disease, heart failure, blood thinners, aspirin or other NSAIDs, aspirin-sensitive asthma, pregnancy (unless a doctor advises), snakebite or bleeding. Aspirin Suspected heart attack (chest pressure or pain, often spreading to arm, jaw or back; sweating; breathlessness) Chew 162–325 mg once (e.g. 2–4 low-dose 81 mg tablets, or one 300–325 mg tablet) — only if not allergic, no bleeding problems, and ideally on the advice …

t: Positive ID or don't use Only use a plant you can identify with complete certainty — see Foraging. These are comfort measures, not cures. Clean wounds properly first; never put plant material into deep or dirty wounds. Test on a small patch of skin; stop if it itches or reddens. Avoid plants from sprayed lawns and roadsides.

s: Plantago major (broadleaf) · P. lanceolata (ribwort) · skin use
f: Common plantain Plantago major (broadleaf) · P. lanceolata (ribwort) · skin use
t: ID: low rosette on lawns, paths and field edges. Broadleaf: oval leaves; ribwort: narrow, lance-shaped leaves. Both have strong parallel veins that pull out as stringy threads when you tear a leaf, and stiff leafless stalks topped with a spike of tiny flowers. Use: crush or bruise a clean leaf until juicy and hold it on a sting, bite, itchy spot or minor scrape (after cleaning). Replace as it dries. Traditional use; lab studies suggest mild anti-inflammatory effects, clinical evidence is limited. Lily-of-the-valley (poisonous) also has parallel-veined leaves. Plantain grows as a flat rosette with a stiff flower spike — if unsure, don't.

s: Gel only · minor burns and sunburn
f: Aloe vera Gel only · minor burns and sunburn
t: Use: after cooling a minor burn for 20 minutes, cut a leaf, let the yellow sap drain away, and apply the clear inner gel to minor (superficial) burns and sunburn. Gel only: the yellow latex just under the skin is an irritant and laxative. Rinse it off. Not on deep, large, blistered or open burns. Not to be eaten. Some people are allergic — test a small patch. Agave (common in the Algarve and other dry places) looks similar and its sap irritates skin. Be sure it's aloe: soft, fleshy, gel-filled leaves.

s: Impatiens capensis / pallida · poison ivy (weak evidence)
f: Jewelweed Impatiens capensis / pallida · poison ivy (weak evidence)
t: North American plant of damp, shady ground; orange or yellow hanging flowers; juicy, translucent stems. Crushed stem juice is a traditional remedy for poison ivy. Evidence is weak — studies found it no better than washing with soap. What actually works: wash the skin with soap and plenty of water as soon as possible after contact (and wash clothes and tools), then hydrocortisone cream for the itch.

s: Salix species · aspirin-like pain relief — same cautions as aspirin
f: Willow bark Salix species · aspirin-like pain relief — same cautions as aspirin
t: Willow bark contains salicin, which the body converts into a relative of aspirin. Traditionally the inner bark of young branches is made into a bitter tea for aches and fever. Same cautions as aspirin Not for children or teens under 19 (Reye's), pregnancy or breastfeeding, aspirin/NSAID allergy or aspirin-sensitive asthma, blood thinners or bleeding problems, stomach ulcers, kidney disease. Don't combine with aspirin or ibuprofen. The amount of salicin varies hugely between trees — you can't know the dose.

s: Identification risk
f: Why yarrow isn't recommended here Identification risk
t: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) has a long traditional history on minor cuts. But its feathery leaves and flat clusters of small white flowers are confused by beginners with poison hemlock and water hemlock — among the most poisonous plants in the Northern Hemisphere. The small benefit isn't worth that risk unless you are already an expert at telling them apart.

Bleeding: commercial tourniquet (CAT / SOF-T Wide), hemostatic or compressed gauze, pressure bandage, nitrile gloves, trauma shears Wounds: irrigation syringe, sterile gauze pads, non-stick dressings, wound-closure strips, adhesive bandages, medical tape, fine-tipped tweezers, safety pins Blisters: moleskin or blister dressings, smooth tape Splints: SAM splint, elastic bandage, 2 triangular bandages Environment: emergency blanket or bivvy bag, chemical heat packs, instant cold pack, ORS packets Medicines: see table; personal prescriptions, epinephrine and inhalers if prescribed Other: CPR face shield or pocket mask, thermometer, headlamp, permanent marker (tourniquet time, swelling edges), notebook and pencil, whistle, duct tape Know how to use everything in it. Check expiry dates every few months.

Any tourniquet, or bleeding that isn't controlled Chest pain; difficulty breathing; anaphylaxis (even if better after epinephrine) Unresponsive, confused, seizure, or head injury red flags Signs of shock Moderate/severe hypothermia; heat stroke; frostbite beyond frostnip Serious burns (see Burns), electrical or chemical burns, airway burns Suspected spinal injury; open fracture; thigh or pelvis fracture; fracture with poor circulation; dislocation Deep or gaping wounds; bites; punctures to hands, feet or joints; signs of infection Snakebite; any bite with rabies risk Bloody diarrhoea, severe dehydration, can't keep fluids down Eye injury affecting vision, or anything stuck in the eye Severe or worsening belly pain; pregnancy complications When in doubt, go early — in daylight, while the patient can still help and the weather allows.

Getting protein in an emergency, cleaning it safely, and making food last. Water and shelter come first; food is a slower problem. For wild plant foods see Foraging; for drinking water see Water. Hunting, trapping and fishing laws apply to you unless your life is genuinely at risk. Food-preservation mistakes can kill (botulism) — follow tested recipes exactly. When in doubt, throw it out.

You can go weeks without food (rule of 3s, typical not absolute: 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in harsh weather, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food). Sort out water and shelter first. Calories matter more than variety. Fat and carbohydrate (oil, nuts, grains, sugar) keep you warm and moving. Eat your stored food sensibly before gambling energy on wild food. Count the cost. Hunting, trapping and fishing burn calories. A day's effort can easily yield less than it costs — especially for beginners. Short on water? Eat sparingly, especially protein, which needs extra water to process. Don't get sick from your food. Vomiting and diarrhoea cost water and strength you can't spare. Cook thoroughly; wash hands. "Rabbit starvation" (protein poisoning) Living on very lean meat alone — rabbit, squirrel, lean fish — without enough fat or carbohydrate causes nausea, diarrhoea, weakness and intense cravings, and you can starve while eating. Eat the fat, marrow and organs (liver, heart, kidneys) of healthy animals, and add fat or starch from any other source: oils, nuts, stored grains, starchy plants.

Legal warning — read first Trapping and snaring are illegal or tightly regulated in most places outside a genuine life-or-death emergency. Licences, seasons, permitted trap types, protected species and landowner permission all apply. Snares are indiscriminate. They catch pets, deer, protected species — and can injure people. Check every trap at least once a day. Leaving an animal suffering is cruel and, in most places, an offence. Dispatch catches quickly and humanely (a fast, firm blow to the back of the head for small game). Know where every set is. Remove them all when you leave. Be honest about the odds: beginners usually catch little or nothing. Experienced trappers set many traps to get a few animals. Trapping only pays if you set several, at fresh sign, and check them daily — so it works best alongside fishing and plant foods, not instead of them.

Runs and trails: narrow, worn paths through grass and brush, under fences and fallen logs. Fresh = vegetation still bent, no cobwebs across it. Droppings: fresh ones are moist and dark. Rabbits leave small round pellets in clusters. Tracks in mud, sand and snow; feeding sign: gnawed bark, cleanly clipped twigs, opened nut shells. Dens and burrows, and the routes between bedding, feeding and water. Animals use the same paths daily, often at dawn and dusk. Funnels: places where the landscape narrows the route — gaps between rocks or bushes, under a leaning log, along a fence line, a narrow bank by water.

Set traps where the animal has to pass. Use natural funnels first. Add a few sticks or bits of brush either side of the set to close gaps, so the easiest route is through the trap. Change as little as possible: disturbed ground, fresh-cut wood and human scent make animals detour. Work quickly, and handle sets with gloves or soil-rubbed hands.

View looking along the run, as the animal approaches. Loop and gap each about a fist (≈ 4 in / 10 cm) for rabbit-sized animals. Find an active run with fresh sign, ideally at a natural narrow point. Make the noose: twist a small eye in one end of flexible snare wire (brass or stainless). Pass the other end through the eye to form a loop that slides freely. Size it: loop about a fist wide (≈ 4 in / 10 cm) for rabbit; bottom of the loop about a fist above the ground. Hang it across the run, facing along the trail, from a crossbar or anchor that is firmly fixed — a caught animal pulls hard. Close side gaps with guide sticks so the loop is the easiest way through. Check at least daily. Dispatch quickly. Remove or spring every snare when you are done.

Three notched sticks hold up a heavy flat rock. An animal tugging the bait collapses the sticks and the rock drops. It works without wire, but takes practice to carve and tune. Assembled, side view. The circles mark where the sticks lock: the diagonal rests on the upright's top; its lower end is held by the trigger; the trigger locks against a notch in the upright. The bait end sits under the rock. The three parts. Highlighted bands show where to cut each notch. Carve the notches so the pieces lock together firmly but slip apart with a light touch on the bait. Cut three straight, dry, sound sticks. Thicker sticks for a heavier rock. Upright: carve the top to a flat chisel edge. Cut a square notch on one side, partway down, at trigger height. Diagonal: cut a notch near its top end so it sits on the upright's chisel top. Carve its lower end to a chisel edge. Trigger: cut a notch near one end to take the diagonal's chisel end, and a square notch where it crosses the upright so the two lock. Sharpen the other end for bait. Practise without the rock until it holds together and collapses at a light touch on the bait end. Set it by an active run. Lean a heavy flat rock (or log) so its raised edge rests on the diagonal's top and the bait end is under the rock. Close the sides with sticks so the animal must reach in from the front. Fingers and hands Deadfalls trip while you set them. Keep your hands, arms and head out from under the rock at all times — support it from the side and …

t: Legal warning Most places require a fishing licence and set seasons, size limits and catch limits. Set lines and trotlines, fish traps, spears and gigs, gorges, nets and night fishing are often restricted or banned, and live fish as bait is often banned (it spreads invasive species and disease). Check local rules. Never use poisons — plant or chemical — or explosives: illegal nearly everywhere, they kill everything downstream and can poison you.

h: Hand line on a bottle or stick
f: Hand line on a bottle or stick
t: Tie the line to the neck of a plastic bottle (or a can or stick) and wind it neatly around the body. Tie on a hook. Add a small weight a little above it (stone, nut, split shot) and a float if you want one (stick, cork, bit of foam). Cast: point the bottle's neck at your target and swing the weighted rig out — the line spirals off the end of the bottle like a spinning reel. With a stick, lay loose coils on clear ground and toss the rig. Retrieve by winding line back onto the bottle. Hold the line over a finger to feel bites; set the hook with a firm pull. Line: fishing line from your kit, dental floss, strong thread, or the thin inner strands pulled from paracord.

Line shown in the highlight colour. A gorge is baited lengthwise; when the fish swallows it, a pull on the line turns it crosswise and it lodges. Gorge: a sliver of bone or hard wood, about 1 in (2–3 cm) long for small fish (longer for bigger fish), sharpened at both ends, with a groove at the middle for the line. Bait it lengthwise. Let the fish swallow it before pulling. It usually kills the fish — no catch-and-release — and is banned in many places. Thorn hook: cut a twig with a stout thorn (hawthorn, blackthorn) so the thorn points back up the shank; tie the line at the top. Safety pin, paperclip or wire: bend into a J, sharpen the point on a stone. A pin's spring loop makes a ready eye. Carved bone or hard wood hooks work but take time; keep them small.

Worms: dig in damp, rich soil; look under logs and stones after rain. Insects: grasshoppers, crickets, beetles; grubs from rotting logs. Fish scraps: eyes, guts and strips of belly from your first catch. Check its stomach to see what the fish are eating and copy that.

Eddies and slack water behind rocks and logs; the seam where fast water meets slow. Undercut banks, shade under overhanging trees, sunken wood and weed edges. Drop-offs, deep pools, and where a riffle runs into a pool. Inflows and outlets of lakes. Dawn and dusk are best. In hot weather fish go deeper and cooler; in cold weather they sit in slow, deep water. Move quietly, keep your shadow off the water, and stay back from the edge.

A line with several baited hooks left in place — stretched between two anchors, or tied to a springy branch pushed into the bank. They fish while you do other work. Often regulated or banned — check the law. Check them at least daily (morning and evening is better), mark where they are, and remove every line and hook when you leave — abandoned lines kill birds, turtles and mammals.

Bottle trap: catches minnows and small fish — good bait, or food in quantity. Cut a large clear plastic bottle just below the shoulder. Remove the cap. Turn the top around and push it into the body so the neck points inward. Fasten with string, thorns or pins through both layers. Punch small holes so water flows through and it sinks. Bait it (bread, fish scraps, crushed snails), weight it with a stone, and set it in slow, shallow water near cover, tied to the bank. Check it every few hours. Fish find the funnel going in, but rarely find the narrow exit. Stick funnel trap, top view. The funnel's narrow end must stick into the pen so trapped fish swim around the walls and miss the exit. In shallow water at the edge of a stream or lake, drive straight sticks or canes firmly into the bottom in a ring — gaps narrower than the fish you want. Leave one side open and build a funnel of stakes leading into it: wide at the mouth, with a narrow gap that ends inside the pen. Fill gaps at the bottom with stones; bait the pen if you like. Check it often. Close the gap with a stick and scoop fish out by hand or with a shirt used as a net.

Split the end of a straight sapling into 2–4 prongs, wedge them apart, and sharpen them (barbs help). Lashing on a knife risks losing it. Refraction: fish are deeper than they look. Aim low, below the fish you see. Approach slowly, keep still, strike from close. Success rates are low, and wading in cold or fast water is dangerous. Spearing is banned for many species and waters. Fish and shellfish that can poison you Don't eat fish from polluted water — below mines, industry, sewage outfalls or heavy farmland, or where advisories are posted. Wild mussels, clams and oysters: only from waters officially open for harvest. Algal toxins ("red tide") are not destroyed by cooking and can cause fatal paralysis. Never eat pufferfish. Large tropical reef fish can carry ciguatera toxin, also not destroyed by cooking.

Kill quickly with a sharp blow to the top of the head behind the eyes. Cutting the gills to bleed it improves the meat. Keep it cool — shade, wet cloth, cold water — and clean it promptly. Scale if you'll eat the skin: scrape from tail to head with the back of a knife. Trout and small fish don't need it. Gut: put the knife point in the vent (small hole near the tail fin) and slit the belly forward to the gills, shallow so you don't cut the guts. Pull the guts out. Remove the gills — they spoil fastest. Scrape out the bloodline (dark red strip along the backbone) with a thumbnail or spoon. Rinse in clean water. Fresh fish: clear, bulging eyes; red or pink gills; firm flesh that springs back; mild smell. Throw it out if eyes are sunken and cloudy, gills brown or grey, flesh soft, or it smells sour or of ammonia. Cook thoroughly until the flesh is opaque and flakes — 145 °F (63 °C) inside. Freshwater fish carry parasites: never eat them raw.

Tularemia and sick animals Wear gloves (nitrile or rubber) when cleaning rabbits and hares — tularemia (rabbit fever) infects through skin cuts, eyes and mouth. Don't touch your face. Don't eat any animal that acted sick — sluggish, easy to catch, staggering, mangy. Wash hands and tools well afterwards. Gloves on. Work on a clean surface away from your water source. Skin: pinch up the skin in the middle of the back and cut a small slit across it. Hook two fingers of each hand in and pull apart, toward the head and the tail. Cut off the head, feet and tail. (Squirrel skin is tougher; cut more and pull hard.) Gut: lay it on its back. Pinch up the belly wall and make a shallow cut. Guard the blade with two fingers inside and open from the pelvis to the ribs without puncturing the intestines or bladder — their contents taint the meat. Pull out the guts. Lift the bladder out intact. Cut around the vent to free the end of the gut. Check the liver: it should be smooth and evenly dark red-brown. White or yellow spots → discard the whole animal (bury or burn it) and scrub hands and tools. Discard also if the meat smells bad or has abscesses. Keep the heart, kidneys and a healthy liver — valuable fat and nutrients. Rinse with clean water and cool the meat fast: hang it in shade, or put it in a sealed bag in cold water. In warm weather cook or preserve it within hours. Bury guts and skins well away from camp and water.

h: Safe cooking temperatures (inside the thickest part)
f: Safe cooking temperatures (inside the thickest part)
t: Food Minimum Fish 145 °F (63 °C) — opaque, flakes easily Wild game, minced meat, bear and wild boar 160 °F (71 °C) — no pink, juices clear Poultry and wild birds 165 °F (74 °C) No thermometer: cook small game until no pink remains anywhere, including at the bone, and juices run clear. Bear, boar and other carnivore meat can carry trichinella that survives freezing — always cook it through.

High in protein and fat, and easier to catch than game. Grasshoppers, crickets, ants, termites, and beetle larvae (grubs from rotting wood) are common choices. Cook all insects — roast, boil or fry — to kill parasites and germs. Pull off the legs and wings of grasshoppers and crickets (spiny legs can stick in the throat). Start with a small amount: people allergic to shellfish or dust mites may react to insects. Avoid brightly coloured, hairy or fuzzy, and foul-smelling insects, and caterpillars in general. Never eat ticks, flies or mosquitoes (disease carriers), or insects from areas sprayed with pesticide.

Germs and moulds need moisture, warmth, low acid and time. Every method takes one or more away: drying (water), salt (water), acid (fermenting, pickling), cold (cellar, cold water, snow), and heat plus a seal (canning). Smoke adds flavour and dries the surface — on its own it preserves very little. The danger zone: 40–140 °F (4–60 °C) Bacteria multiply fast in this range. Don't leave fresh meat, fish or cooked food in it for more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90 °F / 32 °C). Cook it, chill it, or start preserving it.

Choose lean meat and trim off every bit of visible fat — fat goes rancid. Partly freeze it for easier slicing. Slice thin, about 1/4 in (6 mm), against the grain. Marinate in the fridge or another cold place (salt, soy sauce, spices). Throw used marinade away. Heat the meat to 160 °F (71 °C) — poultry 165 °F (74 °C) — before drying (for example, simmer the strips in the marinade until they reach that temperature), or after drying if your tested recipe heats it then. This kills germs that low drying temperatures don't. Dry at 130–140 °F (54–60 °C) with good airflow — dehydrator, oven with the door propped open, or a carefully managed drying rack by the fire. Keep that temperature through the whole drying time. Done when a cooled piece bends and cracks, but doesn't snap. Blot off fat beads, cool, and pack in airtight containers or bags. Storage: about 1–2 months at room temperature in an airtight container; longer in a fridge or freezer. Mould, slime or a rancid smell: discard. Sun and air drying meat Sun or air drying can't reliably reach safe temperatures and is slow in humid weather — meat can spoil before it dries. Heat the meat to 160 °F (71 °C) first. Wild game, especially bear and boar, must reach 160 °F.

Use ripe, sound produce. Wash, peel if needed, and slice thin and even. Light-coloured fruit (apples, pears, peaches, bananas): dip slices briefly in diluted lemon juice (or a vitamin C solution) to slow browning. Most vegetables need brief blanching (steam or boil) before drying to stop enzyme changes — use the times in a tested drying guide. Dry at about 130–140 °F (54–60 °C) with airflow. A solar dehydrator (dark box, screen trays, vents, covered from insects) works in dry, sunny weather. Fruit is done when leathery and pliable with no moisture when squeezed; vegetables when brittle or crisp. Condition fruit: pack loosely in a closed jar for about a week, shaking daily. Any moisture on the glass → dry it more. Store airtight, cool, dark and dry.

Hot smoking — use this Smokes and cooks at once (USDA: smoker around 225–300 °F / 107–149 °C). Cook to an internal 145 °F (63 °C) for fish and 160 °F (71 °C) for game. Cold smoking — not for beginners Smoke below cooking temperature flavours food but does not cook it. Without correct curing salts and a tested recipe it is a real botulism and listeria risk, especially for fish. Hot-smoked food is cooked food, not shelf-stable Eat it within a few days, keep it cold, or freeze it — or dry it fully as jerky. Never seal home-smoked fish airtight and keep it at room temperature (botulism).

Clear the ground of anything flammable. Never smoke food inside a tent or closed shelter — carbon monoxide kills. Lash three poles into a tripod roughly head height. Build a rack of green, non-toxic sticks across it at about waist height above a small fire pit. Salt or brine the meat or fish per a tested recipe, then lay thin strips or split fish on the rack. Wrap the tripod in a tarp, canvas, bark or brush, leaving a small gap at the top for draught. Keep a small, low, steady fire — coals topped with green or damp hardwood chips for smoke. Watch for flare-ups. Check internal temperature in the thickest piece (145 °F / 63 °C fish, 160 °F / 71 °C game). No thermometer: cook until fully opaque and firm throughout, then treat it as cooked food. A long trench or pipe between the fire and the chamber cools the smoke — that is a cold-smoking design. Skip it unless you already know safe cold smoking.

Good: hardwoods — oak, hickory, maple, beech, alder, apple, cherry and other fruit woods. No resinous softwoods (pine, spruce, fir) — sooty, bitter. No treated, painted, varnished or glued wood, plywood, or pallets of unknown origin. No poisonous plants: oleander, yew, poison ivy/oak/sumac, laurels — or any wood you can't identify.

Very fresh fish only. Gut it, remove the head, split it flat, scrape out the bloodline, rinse and drain. Always gut first. Use plenty of pure salt — coarse, pickling or sea salt without additives. In a non-metal container (food-grade plastic, wood, glazed crock): a layer of salt, a layer of fish skin-side down, salt over every surface, and repeat. Finish with salt. Put a weight on top and keep it as cool as you can. The salt draws out water as brine. Leave for days to weeks depending on thickness and temperature, adding salt if bare patches appear, until the flesh is firm and translucent all the way through. Brush off the salt and dry the fish in a cool, breezy, covered place, protected from rain, dew and flies, until stiff. Store wrapped, cool and dry. Never salt-cure ungutted fish Whole, ungutted salted or dried fish have caused fatal botulism outbreaks. Gut it first, keep it cold while the salt works, and discard anything slimy, pink-tinged, mouldy or off-smelling.
Soaking in salty water adds flavour and helps before smoking or drying. Brine alone does not make meat shelf-stable — keep brining meat cold and follow a tested recipe.

Nitrite is toxic in excess Proper meat curing (ham, bacon, sausages, anything cold-smoked) uses nitrite curing salt ("Cure #1", "Prague powder") in exact amounts from a tested recipe, weighed on a scale. Too little risks botulism; too much is poisonous. Never guess the dose. Curing salt is often dyed pink — don't confuse it with table salt or pink Himalayan salt, and keep it away from children.

Soak salted fish or meat in cold water, kept cold, changing the water several times — about a day or two for thick salt fish. Taste a small cooked piece. Very salty food needs extra drinking water: don't eat it when water is short.

Most root crops keep best at roughly 32–40 °F (0–4 °C) and 85–95% humidity, dark, with some ventilation. Don't let them freeze. Crop Conditions Notes Potatoes Cold, humid, dark Cure first (below). Light turns them green — cut away green parts and sprouts, which are toxic. Carrots, beets, turnips, parsnips Cold, humid Twist off tops leaving a short stub. Pack in damp sand, sawdust or leaves. Cabbage Cold, humid Strong smell — keep it away from apples, or store it outside the cellar in a clamp. Apples, pears Cold, humid Keep away from potatoes, carrots and cabbage: their ethylene gas makes potatoes sprout and carrots bitter. Onions, garlic Cool and dry Not in a damp cellar. Cure (dry) skins well first; hang in mesh. Winter squash, pumpkins, sweet potatoes Warmer, about 50–60 °F (10–15 °C), and drier Too cold damages them. A cool room or closet, not the cellar. Store only mature, undamaged produce. Don't wash — brush off soil. Use bruised or cut pieces first. Cure potatoes in the dark at moderate temperature for about 2 weeks so skins toughen and nicks heal. Ventilate: cold air in low, warm air out high. In autumn, open vents on cold nights and close them on warm days. Check every week. Remove anything soft, sprouting, mouldy or rotting — rot spreads. Watch for rodents.

Buried container: sink a clean barrel or bin (food-grade if produce touches it) on its side or upright in well-drained ground, rim just above the surface. Layer produce with straw or dry leaves, lid on, then heap soil and straw over the top. Dig a drain trench around it. Clamp (pit): see diagram. Clamp, cross-section. Pile roots in a cone on straw, cover with a thick layer of straw, then soil, leaving a straw tuft at the top for ventilation. Dig a trench around it so water drains away. In mild-winter climates (such as southern Portugal) the ground and air rarely get cold enough. Expect much shorter storage, and eat the most perishable crops first.

The rule that matters Water-bath canning is ONLY for high-acid foods (pH 4.6 or lower): most fruits, jams, pickles, and tomatoes with added acid. Low-acid foods — vegetables, meat, fish, beans, soups — must be pressure canned. Use tested recipes (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning / National Center for Home Food Preservation). This page deliberately gives no processing times: they depend on the food, jar size, packing method and altitude, and must come from a tested recipe. Botulism spores survive boiling. In high-acid food they can't grow; in low-acid food sealed without oxygen they can, making a deadly toxin with no smell or taste. That is why acidity and method must match a tested recipe — don't add extra onions, peppers or other low-acid ingredients to one.

Pick a tested recipe. Note its processing time, jar size, headspace and altitude adjustments before you start. Jars: proper canning jars with no chips or cracks. New flat lids every time (bands can be reused). Wash in hot soapy water and keep jars hot. If the recipe's processing time is under 10 minutes, sterilise the empty jars first (boil 10 minutes, plus 1 minute for each 1,000 ft / 300 m above 1,000 ft). Prepare the food exactly as written. Acidify tomatoes with bottled lemon juice or citric acid as directed (bottled juice has consistent acidity). Fill hot jars, leaving the headspace in the recipe (commonly 1/4 in / 6 mm for jams and jellies, 1/2 in / 12 mm for fruit, tomatoes and pickles). Remove air bubbles with a non-metal utensil. Wipe rims clean, put on lids, screw bands fingertip-tight. Jars on a rack in the canner, covered by at least 1 in (2.5 cm) of water. Lid on the canner. Start timing at a full rolling boil and keep it boiling. If the boil stops, bring it back and restart the time from zero. Altitude: above 1,000 ft (300 m), increase the time using the recipe's altitude table. When time is up, turn off the heat, remove the canner lid, wait 5 minutes, then lift jars straight up onto a towel, spaced apart, out of draughts. Leave undisturbed for 12–24 hours. Don't tighten bands or tip jars. Check seals: the lid is curved down and doesn't flex when pressed. Unsealed jars: refrigerate and eat soon, or reprocess within 24 hours with a new lid. t: Low-acid foods need temperatures only a pressure canner reaches. Use a tested recipe for time and pressure, adjust for altitude, and have a dial gauge tested every year. Electric pressure cookers and multicookers are not recommended for canning. Unsafe methods — never use Water-bath or "boiling" for low-acid foods (vegetables, meat, fish, beans, soups) Open-kettle canning — filling hot jars and sealing without processing Oven canning, microwave or dishwasher "canning" Inversion — turning jars upside down to seal them Untested, made-up or very old recipes and times Botulism — warning signs and symptoms Jar warning signs: bulging or swollen lid, leaking, unsealed, liquid spurting when opened, foaming, mould, cloudy liquid in a normally clear product, or an off smell. Many contaminated jars look and smell normal. Symptoms, usually 12–36 hours after eating (can be a few hours to about 10 days): blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, dry mouth, muscle weakness, difficulty breathing, and paralysis that spreads downward from the head. This is a medical emergency — call 911/112 immediately. Antitoxin works best early. Never taste food to test it. A tiny amount can kill. Discard bulging, leaking or spurting jars without opening or tasting. Wear gloves, seal them in a heavy bag, and dispose of them where people and animals can't reach them. Wash hands and any surfaces they touched. When in doubt, throw it out.

Use fresh, clean vegetables and a glass, food-grade plastic or glazed crock container — not metal, and not old crocks that may have lead glaze. Salt at about 2–3% by weight: a 2–3% brine is 20–30 g salt per litre of water. For shredded cabbage, mix the salt in and pound until it releases its own juice. Keep everything under the brine — weight it with a plate and a clean stone or a water-filled bag. Exposed vegetables go mouldy. Ferment at cool room temperature, covered to keep insects out, for days to weeks until pleasantly sour. Then store cold (fridge, cellar, cold water), still under brine. Normal: bubbles, cloudy brine, sour smell, a thin white film on the surface (skim it off). Discard if there is fuzzy, pink or black mould through the food, the vegetables are soft or slimy, or it smells rotten.

Use vinegar labelled at least 5% acidity. Never dilute it more than the recipe says — the acid is the safety margin. Homemade vinegar has unknown strength: don't use it for canned pickles. Use canning/pickling salt and a tested recipe. For shelf storage, process in a water bath per the recipe. Unprocessed "refrigerator pickles" must stay cold.

How to find, identify, pick and process wild nuts and fruit in the temperate north-east US (New Jersey, USDA zones 6–7) and the Mediterranean (Algarve, Portugal). Conservative by design: when in doubt, leave it. If you are not 100% sure of the identification, do not eat it Confirm every plant with a regional field guide and, ideally, a local expert. Check several features (leaf, bark, flower, fruit, seed, habitat), not just one. This app is a reference, not a positive ID. Never eat white berries, or any berry you cannot name. Never eat wild mushrooms based on this page. Fungi are out of scope. Even with a known, safe food, try a small amount first and wait several hours before eating more. Allergies: anyone allergic to one tree nut may react to others. Chestnut and fig can cross-react with latex allergy. Know who in your group has allergies and where their epinephrine auto-injector is. Don't pick near roads, rail lines, power-line corridors, sprayed fields, orchards or lawns, golf courses, industrial sites, dumps or polluted water. Pick above knee height (dogs). Don't make anyone vomit unless told to. Full steps Reference only. Written descriptions can't replace hands-on identification by an expert. Most nuts are ripe when they fall on their own. These rules apply to every nut: Collect often, daily if you can. Squirrels, mould and insects take nuts left on the ground. Discard nuts with small round holes (weevil exits), cracks or mould, and any that feel light for their size. Float test (acorns, hulled walnuts, hickory, chestnuts, hazelnuts): tip them into a bucket of water. Floaters are usually empty or wormy, so throw them out. Sinkers are usually good. The test isn't perfect, so still check every kernel. Mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured kernels can carry aflatoxin, a liver toxin that cooking doesn't destroy. When in doubt, throw it out. Kill hidden larvae: freeze nuts for at least 48 hours at 0 °F (−18 °C) before storing.

Where NE US: forests, parks, old fields, everywhere. Algarve: inland hills and cork-oak woodland (Serra do Caldeirão, Monchique). When NE US: Sep–Nov, peak Oct. Algarve: Oct–Jan. t: Husk stains: wear gloves Very hard shell Identify Large tree. Leaves are 1–2 ft (30–60 cm) long and compound, with 15–23 narrow, toothed leaflets. The end leaflet is often small or missing. t: Horse chestnut and buckeyes are toxic Horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) is a common park and street tree in Europe and the US, and native US buckeyes are the same genus. Eating them causes vomiting and diarrhoea, and larger amounts cause muscle twitching, weakness and collapse. Children are most at risk. They are not edible raw, roasted or boiled. Never taste-test to tell the two apart. How to tell sweet chestnut from toxic horse chestnut Feature Sweet chestnut (edible, cooked) Horse chestnut / buckeye (TOXIC) Husk Dense, sharp, needle-like spines all over, like a hedgehog Thick, leathery husk with a few short spikes, warts, or smooth Nuts per husk Usually 2–3 Usually 1 (sometimes 2) Nut shape Flattened on one or two sides, with a pointed tip and a small tassel Round, smooth, very glossy, with a large pale circular scar. No point, no tassel. Leaves Single long leaf with bristle-tipped teeth Palmate: 5–7 leaflets spreading from one point, like the fingers of a hand Flowers Long, creamy, stringy catkins (early summer) Upright "candles" of white or pink flowers (spring) Check all three: husk, nut and leaf. If any one doesn't match sweet chestnut, don't eat it.

t: Containers: shallow baskets or rigid tubs for soft fruit. A bucket hung from your belt or neck leaves both hands free. Use mesh or cloth bags for nuts so air can flow. Avoid closed plastic bags for anything warm or wet. Tarp or old sheet, about 10 × 10 ft (3 × 3 m), for shaking. Long pole (bamboo or similar) for tapping branches. A hooked stick (a forked branch or a cane with a hook) for gently pulling branches down. Gloves: leather for chestnut burs, brambles and prickly pear; waterproof nitrile or rubber for walnut husks and fig sap. Tongs (prickly pear), pruners or scissors (grape, elderberry and loquat clusters), and a small knife. Hand rake or leaf rake to pull nuts out of leaf litter. A rolling nut gatherer (a wire cage on a handle) picks up walnuts, pecans, chestnuts and acorns without bending. A hat and eye protection when shaking trees. Long sleeves and trousers, insect repellent and water.

Spread the tarp under the branch, out to the edge of the canopy. Clear away sticks and stones so nothing bruises. Put on a hat and eye protection, and stand clear of where things will fall. Shake the branch by hand, or tap it sharply with the pole near the fruit or nuts. Ripe nuts and fruit drop and unripe ones stay, which is the point. Don't thrash or break limbs, because that damages next year's crop. Gather up the corners and pour the harvest into containers. Pick out leaves, unripe fruit, and anything mouldy or holed. Shaking works best for mulberries, serviceberries, almonds, carob, pecans and beechnuts. Gathering from the ground is better for nuts and fruit that drop on their own as they ripen (acorns, walnuts, hickory, chestnuts, pawpaw, persimmon), because you get only ripe ones. Go daily or every other day: whatever lies around gets mouldy, wormy or eaten. Skip anything that has sat in wet leaves for days. Pick by hand soft fruit that bruises (berries, figs, loquat, medronho), and hazelnuts before they fall. Falls are the commonest foraging injury Don't climb trees to forage. Use a stable stepladder only on level ground and with a helper. Never shake a branch you are standing under.

Take no more than about a third of what's on a plant or patch, and less if the patch is small. Spread your picking out. Leave plenty for wildlife. Nuts and fruit are their winter food. Don't damage plants. No breaking branches, stripping bark or pulling up roots. Get permission on private land. In Portugal, olives, almonds, carob, figs, chestnuts and pine cones usually belong to a landowner, even on unfenced, untidy land. Protected areas have rules on collecting: limits or outright bans. That includes many US state and national parks, and Portugal's natural parks (e.g. Ria Formosa, Costa Vicentina). Check before you pick, and never take rare or protected plants.

Roadsides (exhaust, old lead, de-icing salt, herbicide), rail lines and power-line corridors (herbicide), sprayed fields and orchards, lawns, golf courses and parks, industrial sites, dumps and mine spoil, ditches and floodplains that take sewage or polluted runoff, and dog-walking edges. Wash everything in clean water.

Sun drying works in hot, dry, sunny weather, such as an Algarve summer (figs, carob, almonds). Lay produce in a single layer on screens or racks off the ground, under fine mesh against insects and birds. Turn it daily and bring it in at night, because dew re-wets it. It takes days. Solar dryer: a box with a dark base, a clear lid and screened vents top and bottom. Faster and cleaner than open sun. Air drying in shade suits nuts in the shell. Use screens or mesh bags somewhere cool, dry, airy and safe from rodents. Low oven, or near a stove: use the lowest setting with the door propped open, and stir often. Fruit and fruit leather dry well at 135–140 °F (57–60 °C). Dry nuts below about 100 °F (38 °C), because more heat speeds rancidity. Roasting is a separate, final step. When is it done? Dried fruit is leathery with no moist centre when squeezed; nut kernels snap rather than bend. Then condition dried fruit: pack it loosely in a jar and shake daily for a week. Any condensation means it needs more drying.

Fresh fruit: keep in the fridge at 32–40 °F (0–4 °C), unwashed, in shallow containers. Most berries last 1–3 days; figs, mulberries and medronho 1–2. Chestnuts: keep in the fridge in a breathable bag, and use within a few weeks. Freezing: spread berries on a tray, freeze, then bag them so they stay loose. Freeze persimmon and pawpaw as seedless pulp, chestnuts cooked and peeled, and nut kernels in airtight bags (a year or more).

Jam and jelly need enough sugar, acid and pectin to set and keep. Low-sugar jams must be refrigerated or frozen. Low-acid fruits such as figs, mulberries and elderberries need added lemon juice; follow tested recipes. Canning: a water bath is safe only for high-acid foods (pH 4.6 or lower, such as most fruit and jams). Low-acid foods, including olives, need pressure canning. Use tested recipes and read the canning safety rules on the Food page. Throw out bulging, leaking or off-smelling jars without tasting. Fruit leather: purée the fruit, sieve out the seeds, spread it ⅛–¼ in (3–6 mm) thick, and dry until it is no longer sticky. Syrups (elderberry, rose hip, carob): keep in the fridge.

Rancidity: nut oils go rancid with heat, light and air. Rancid nuts smell of paint, crayons or old oil and taste sharp or bitter. Throw them out: they have lost their value and can upset the stomach. Storage: keep nuts in the shell where possible, because the shell protects them. Stored cool, dry, dark and rodent-proof, they last months. Shelled nuts last only weeks at room temperature, months airtight in the fridge, and a year or more in the freezer. Mould: throw out mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured kernels. Mould can produce aflatoxin, which cooking doesn't destroy. Weevils and moth larvae: freeze nuts and dried fruit for at least 48 hours at 0 °F (−18 °C) to kill eggs and larvae, then store airtight. Larvae often crawl out of freshly gathered acorns and chestnuts, so process those quickly.

h: Universal edibility test: last resort only
t: Passing this test does not make a plant safe It is a slow, risky last resort for a genuine survival emergency, and it only screens for fast, obvious reactions. Many plants that pass are still harmful. Some toxins are slow or cumulative: they damage the liver, kidneys or heart, and show up hours or days later, or only after repeated meals. Some plants (water hemlock, yew, oleander, castor bean) are so toxic that even the tiny test amounts can seriously harm or kill. Identification always beats testing.

c: Universal edibility test: last resort only
t: Never on mushrooms or any other fungus. If you have food, can wait for rescue, or can walk out. You can survive about 3 weeks without food; water and shelter matter far more. If you can't spare 24+ hours, or you are already weak. The test costs energy and fluids. On any plant with: milky or discoloured sap; a bitter or soapy taste (if one appears at any step, stop); an almond scent in crushed leaves or woody parts; umbrella-shaped flower clusters, or dill-, carrot- or parsley-like leaves (the deadly carrot family); three-leaved growth (poison ivy and others); beans, bulbs or seeds inside pods; spines, fine hairs or thorns; grain heads with pink, purple or black spurs (ergot); wilted or mouldy parts. On anything you have already identified as toxic, or that resembles a toxic plant on this page. On children, or anyone pregnant or ill.

t: Pick one part to test: leaf, stem, root, bud, flower or fruit. A part that passes says nothing about the plant's other parts, or about the same part prepared another way. Test only plants that are plentiful, or it isn't worth the effort. Smell it. Reject anything with a strong, unpleasant or almond-like smell. Fast for 8 hours before you start. For the whole test, take nothing by mouth except purified water and the plant part you are testing. Skin contact test (do it during the fast): crush the part and hold it against the inside of your elbow or wrist. Watch for burning, itching, redness, rash or swelling for at least 15 minutes, and preferably the whole 8 hours. Any reaction: reject the plant. Prepare a small portion exactly as you plan to eat it, raw or boiled. Each preparation method needs its own test. Lip: touch a small piece to the outer surface of your lip and wait 3 minutes. Any burning, itching, numbness or tingling: stop and reject. Tongue: place a piece on your tongue and hold it there for 15 minutes. Don't chew or swallow. Chew and hold: chew a pinch thoroughly and hold it in your mouth for 15 minutes. Don't swallow. Bitter or soapy taste, burning, stinging or numbness: spit it out, rinse, and reject. Swallow that small amount, then wait 8 hours. Eat nothing else. No reaction at all? Eat a larger amount, about ¼ cup (60 mL), prepared the same way. Wait another 8 hours. t: Signs can start minutes or hours after eating; some much later. Burning, tingling, numbness or swelling of the lips, mouth or throat; drooling, or a very dry mouth. Nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, diarrhoea. Dizziness, headache, sweating, weakness, trembling. Big pupils, blurred vision, hot, dry, flushed skin, confusion, agitation or hallucinations (nightshades, datura). A slow, fast or irregular heartbeat, or fainting (yew, oleander, lily-of-the-valley, foxglove). Muscle twitching or seizures (water hemlock, hemlock water-dropwort). Trouble breathing, hives, or swelling of the face or tongue: this is an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis). On the skin: rash, blisters or burns (fig sap plus sun, glochids, irritant sap). Some poisonings (castor bean, for example) start hours later, after a gap with no symptoms. Don't relax just because someone feels fine.

c: Plant poisoning: signs and what to do
t: Stop eating. Spit out what is in the mouth and rinse with water. Stop everyone else eating the same thing. Call emergency now on 911 (US) or 112 (Portugal/EU) if they have collapsed, are unresponsive, are having seizures, have trouble breathing or chest pain, or have a very slow or irregular pulse. If they have an epinephrine auto-injector and show signs of anaphylaxis, use it. If they are not breathing normally, start CPR (see First aid). If they are unresponsive but breathing, put them in the recovery position. With no signal, try anyway: emergency calls can connect through any network. Otherwise, call poison control right away, even if symptoms are mild: US Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 (24/7, free) · Portugal CIAV 800 250 250. Have ready: the person's age and weight, the plant (or a description), which part, how much, when, and the symptoms. Don't make them vomit unless poison control or a doctor tells you to. No salt water and no fingers down the throat. Give nothing by mouth to anyone drowsy, confused or seizing. Give activated charcoal only if advised to. Keep a sample of the plant (leaves, fruit, seeds) in a bag or paper, and take photos. Keep any vomit too. Bring it all to the hospital. Write down when they ate and when each symptom started. Watch them closely for at least 24 hours, and don't leave them alone. Skin or eyes: remove contaminated clothing and wash skin with soap and plenty of water. Keep fig-sap areas out of the sun. t: No place outside is safe when a thunderstorm is near. Best shelter: an enclosed building with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped metal vehicle with the windows up. Tents, picnic shelters and open sheds offer no protection. Caught outside? These lower the risk a little; they don't make you safe — keep moving toward shelter: Get off peaks, ridges and hilltops. Stay away from isolated tall trees, cliffs and rock overhangs. Get out of and away from water — lakes, rivers, ponds. Stay away from metal fences, power lines and other things that conduct electricity. Don't lie flat on the ground. In a group, spread out so one strike can't injure everyone. The old “lightning crouch” does not make you safe. Use the time to reach shelter. Someone struck? They carry no electric charge — it is safe to touch them. Call for help. If they are not breathing normally, start CPR.

Your phone's GPS works with no phone signal or data. To be found, read rescuers your MGRS grid or latitude/longitude, the accuracy, and what is around you. Read it twice, slowly. Water comes before food: you can last only about 3 days without it. Find the cleanest source you can, clear it, kill the germs, and learn to recognise water that no home method can make safe. For emergencies and learning. These methods lower the risk; none is perfect. Get medical help for severe diarrhoea, vomiting, or signs of severe dehydration.

Drink what you need. Don't ration water. Plan on at least 1 gal (3.8 L) per person per day, and more in heat or hard work. Ration sweat, not water. Pick the cleanest source: rain or spring, then fast-moving stream, then lake, then stagnant water. Never use floodwater, water with a fuel sheen or chemical smell, or water under algae scum. Clear it first: let it settle, then pour it through folded cloth or a filter. Kill the germs: a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m), or unscented bleach (6%: 2 drops per litre, 8 drops per gallon) and wait 30 minutes, or SODIS for 6 hours in full sun. Store it clean and covered in labelled, food-grade containers. Keep dirty and clean containers apart. Boil if in doubt Unsure about a source, a filter or a method? Boil it. A rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft / 2,000 m) kills bacteria, viruses and parasites, including Cryptosporidium, which bleach misses. Boiling does not remove chemicals. If you suspect fuel, metals, pesticides or toxic algae, find another source.

Situation Per person, per day Drinking only, mild weather, resting About 3–4 L (3–4 qt) minimum Heat, hard work, illness, pregnancy or breastfeeding Much more, often double Planning figure (drinking + basic hygiene) 1 gal (3.8 L). That barely covers drinking in mild weather, so store more if you can. How much to store at home At least 3 days' worth; 2 weeks is better. Add extra for pets. Don't ration water. Drink what you need today and look for more tomorrow. Rationing leads to collapse sooner. Ration sweat instead. Work in the cool of morning and evening. Rest in shade. Keep skin covered. Don't drink alcohol. If water is short, eat less, especially salty and high-protein food, because digesting it uses water. Never drink seawater, urine or alcohol. They make dehydration worse. Aim for pale straw-coloured urine.

Stage Signs Do this Early Thirst, dark yellow urine, peeing less, dry mouth, headache, tiredness, irrit­ability Drink now: small sips, often. Rest in shade. Serious Dizziness, very little urine, fast heartbeat, cramps, sunken eyes Stop work. Rehydrate with oral rehydration solution (below). Emergency Confusion, fainting, no urine for many hours, very fast breathing or heartbeat. Babies: dry nappies (diapers) for hours, no tears, sunken soft spot on the head Get medical help. Give sips only if they're fully awake and can swallow. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) Use ORS packets if you have them. Home recipe (WHO): 1 litre of safe water + 6 level teaspoons of sugar + ½ level teaspoon of salt. Stir until dissolved and sip. Measure carefully, because too much salt is harmful. Useful after diarrhoea, vomiting or heavy sweating. For heat illness see First aid.
Think like water: it runs downhill and collects in low, shady places. Save your strength. Wandering in the heat costs more water than it finds.

t: Water heater tank (often 30–80 gal / 110–300 L): turn off the gas or power first. Close the cold-water inlet valve so no contaminated water gets in. Open a hot tap somewhere to let air in, then drain from the valve at the bottom. Let the sediment settle. Careful: it may be scalding hot. Pipes: close the main water valve, open the highest tap in the house, then drain from the lowest tap. Ice cubes, and the liquid in canned fruit and vegetables. If there was a boil-water notice before you closed the supply, treat this water too. Not for drinking: heating radiators and boilers, waterbeds, swimming pools and hot tubs (use them for washing and flushing only).

f: Reading the land clues that point to water
t: Low ground: valley floors, gullies, the foot of cliffs and rock outcrops, shaded hollows. Green lines in dry country: willows, cottonwoods, sycamores, reeds, rushes and cattails grow where water is at or near the surface. Insects: mosquitoes and flies stay near water. Bees fly regularly to and from water. Birds at dawn and dusk: seed-eating birds (doves, pigeons, finches) often fly low and direct towards water. Birds of prey are no guide. Animal trails that converge and lead downhill often end at water. Rock: after rain, look for water held in hollows and cracks in rock. Listen for running water, and for frogs at night. These are clues, not guarantees.

s: often the best natural source
f: Springs often the best natural source
t: Look at the base of slopes and where rock layers meet the ground, often marked by a patch of lush green. Collect right where the water comes out of the ground, before animals or surface run-off can foul it. Dig out a small pool, let it clear, and dip water gently from the top. Still treat it. Clear and cold doesn't mean safe.

h: Dig a seep in a dry stream bed
s: outside of the bend, lowest point
f: Dig a seep in a dry stream bed outside of the bend, lowest point
t: Water lingers longest under the outside of a bend, where the current dug deepest. Damp sand or green plants there are a good sign. Pick the spot: the lowest point on the outside of a bend in a dry stream bed. Look for damp sand or water-loving plants. Dig in the cool of the day, about 30–60 cm (1–2 ft) down, or until the sand turns damp and then a little deeper. If it's still bone-dry after a short dig, try another spot rather than sweat away water. Wait. Water may take minutes to hours to seep in. Let the silt settle, then scoop gently from the top and strain through cloth. Disinfect it (boil or chemicals). On a beach: dig behind the first dune, well above the high-tide line. Fresh water can collect on top of salt water underground. Taste a small sip, and if it's salty, don't drink it. Disinfect before drinking.

s: before sunrise, with cloth
f: Dew collection before sunrise, with cloth
t: Before dawn, tie clean absorbent cloth (cotton or wool) around your shins and walk through tall grass. Or wipe a cloth over grass, leaves, a tarp or a car body. Wring it into a container. Repeat until the dew is gone. That happens soon after sunrise. Disinfect before drinking. Worth doing on heavy-dew mornings, but the yield is often small. Avoid poisonous plants, sprayed crops and roadside verges.

s: clear bag over a leafy branch; small yield
f: Transpiration bags clear bag over a leafy branch; small yield
t: Choose a sunny, leafy branch of a plant you know is non-toxic. Never use poisonous plants such as oleander, yew, or poison ivy, oak or sumac. If you can't identify it, don't use it. Slip a clear plastic bag over the branch. Put a small pebble in one corner to make a low point. Tie the open end tightly around the branch. Leave it in full sun. Water collects in the low corner. Drain it by untying or making a small cut, then retie. Move the bag to fresh leaves each day. Yield is small: often a cupful or less per bag per day, so use several bags. Discard bitter or odd-tasting water.

s: melt first, never eat it when cold
f: Snow and ice melt first, never eat it when cold
t: Never eat snow or ice when you're cold. It steals body heat and pushes you towards hypothermia. Melt it first. Prefer ice to snow. Snow is mostly air, so it takes many potfuls (and lots of fuel) to make one pot of water. Ice gives far more water per pot. Melting snow in a pot: start with a little water in the bottom, then add snow a bit at a time. This keeps the pot from scorching. Without fire: pack snow in a bottle and carry it inside your jacket, between layers (not against bare skin). Use clean white snow away from roads, camps and animal areas. Treat the meltwater like any surface water. Freezing doesn't kill germs.

s: tarp, roof, gutters, first flush
f: Rain capture tarp, roof, gutters, first flush
t: 1 mm of rain on 1 m² = 1 litre 1 in of rain on 1,000 sq ft ≈ 620 gal Measure the roof's footprint (its area seen from above), not its slope. You'll catch somewhat less because of splash and the first flush. Tarp: tie it at the corners with one low point over a clean container. Let the first rain rinse it. Avoid tarps that smell of chemicals. Roof: clean the gutters and screen them against leaves. Let the first few minutes of rain wash the roof before collecting, or fit a first-flush diverter that dumps the dirtiest first water (dust, bird droppings). Collect into covered containers so mosquitoes can't breed and debris can't fall in. Treat roof water before drinking. Rain is clean when it falls, but it picks up germs and dirt from the roof. Roof cautions Best: painted or coated metal, clay or concrete tile, a clean tarp. Use for washing only if you have a better drinking source: asphalt shingles, treated wood shakes, old asbestos-cement sheets, copper roofs or gutters, roofs with lead flashing or old lead paint, and roofs treated with moss killer. Heavy smoke, ash or industrial air pollution can also contaminate rainwater.

Choose the best source you can reach, and treat it anyway. Rank Source Notes 1 Rain (collected cleanly) or a spring at its source Usually the cleanest. Roof water still needs treating. 2 Fast-moving, clear stream Collect upstream of people, farms, livestock, roads and mines. 3 Lake or pond Take it from a clean spot, not the edge where animals drink, and from below the surface. 4 Stagnant water: puddles, ditches, ponds with no outflow Last resort. Settle, filter, then boil. Never Floodwater, fuel or oil sheen, chemical smell, algae scum, near dead animals, mine run-off, below industry No home method fixes it. See why.

If it's cloudy, settle it and strain it through cloth first. Bring it to a rolling boil: big bubbles that keep coming even when you stir. Keep it rolling for 1 minute. Above 6,500 ft (2,000 m), boil for 3 minutes. Let it cool, covered. Don't add ice unless the ice was made from safe water. Store it covered in a clean container. Flat taste? Pour it back and forth between two clean containers, or add a pinch of salt per litre. Boiling longer than this wastes fuel and doesn't make it safer. A lid gets it to the boil faster. Boiling does not remove salt, fuel, metals or other chemicals. No pot? Any clean metal container or can will do. (See Fire & shelter for making fire.)

t: Use the right bleach Use plain, unscented household bleach (sodium hypochlorite). Check the strength on the label: 6% or 8.25%. Do not use scented, "splash-less", colour-safe, or bleach with added cleaners. Bleach weakens with age and heat, so use a fresh bottle if you can. Up to 4 h to kill Crypto­sporidium. Iodine tablets or drops Follow the label Per label; longer if cold For bigger containers, multiply the per-gallon dose by the number of gallons.

t: Settle and filter cloudy water first. Add the drops from the table with a clean dropper. Double them for cloudy, coloured or very cold water. Stir or shake well. Wait at least 30 minutes. Smell it. It should have a slight chlorine smell. If not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. Too strong? Pour it back and forth between two clean containers to air it. Know the limits Bleach does NOT reliably kill Cryptosporidium. Boiling does. Chlorine dioxide can, but needs up to 4 hours. Iodine: not for pregnancy, thyroid problems, iodine allergy, or long-term use (more than a few weeks). Follow the product label. It doesn't kill Cryptosporidium. No chemical removes fuel, metals, pesticides or algae toxins.

Ultraviolet light and heat from the sun kill most germs in clear water in clear bottles. It's free and needs no fuel, but you need clear water and strong sun. Bottle: clear PET plastic (recycling code 1, "PET" or "PETE"), 2 L or smaller. Remove the labels. Replace bottles that are badly scratched or cloudy. Water must be clear. Stand the filled bottle on a newspaper headline and look down through the opening. If you can't read the headline, settle or filter the water first. Fill and cap the bottle. Lay the bottles flat in full sun, ideally on a metal roof or sheet. Make sure nothing will shade them during the day. Leave for 6 hours of full sun. If more than half the sky is cloudy, leave for 2 consecutive days. Drink straight from the bottle or a clean cup. Don't pour it into a dirty container. SODIS limits Don't use it on rainy days. It does nothing for chemicals. It doesn't work in coloured glass or in big containers. When in doubt, boil.
