t: Let cloudy water stand in a bucket until the sediment sinks: 30 minutes for slightly cloudy water, overnight for muddy water. Pour or siphon the clear top water into another container without stirring up the bottom. Pour it through folded clean cloth: several layers of cotton such as a T-shirt or bandana, or a coffee filter. Now disinfect it. Clear water lets boiling, chemicals and sunlight work properly.

c: Filtering: settling, commercial filters, improvised filters
t: Hollow-fibre filters (0.1–0.2 micron) remove bacteria and protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) but not viruses. Water that may carry sewage (near towns, floodwater, farm run-off, countries with poor sanitation) also needs chemical treatment or boiling after filtering. Filters labelled as purifiers are rated to handle viruses as well. Keep them from freezing. A wet filter that freezes can crack with no visible sign. Sleep with it in your sleeping bag in cold weather. If it may have frozen, treat its output with chemicals or boil it, or replace the filter. Keep the dirty and clean sides apart. Backflush as the maker says. Pre-filter muddy water so it doesn't clog. A carbon stage improves taste, but don't rely on it for fuel, metals or algae toxins.

c: Filtering: settling, commercial filters, improvised filters
t: It does not make water safe An improvised sand/charcoal filter improves clarity and taste only. It does NOT make water safe. Always disinfect afterwards (boil, chemicals or SODIS). Water goes in at the top and drips out of the neck. Coarse layers at the bottom stop the fine layers washing out.

c: Filtering: settling, commercial filters, improvised filters › Improvised sand and charcoal filter
s: bottle or bucket
f: Build it, step by step bottle or bucket
t: Container: a large plastic bottle with the bottom cut off, hung upside down with the cap removed. Or a bucket with a small hole near the bottom. Plug the neck or hole with clean cloth or cotton. Make charcoal from your own fire: black, burned-through pieces of untreated wood (not ash, not painted or treated wood, not barbecue briquettes, which contain additives). Crush to pea-size or smaller and rinse out the dust. Rinse the sand and gravel until the rinse water runs fairly clear. Add layers from the bottom up: gravel, coarse sand, crushed charcoal, fine sand, then cloth on top. In a bucket, roughly: gravel 5 cm (2 in), coarse sand 5 cm (2 in), charcoal 5–8 cm (2–3 in), fine sand 10–15 cm (4–6 in). In a bottle, scale down but keep fine sand the thickest layer, and leave room at the top for water. Pour water in slowly so you don't dig holes in the sand. Throw away the first few runs until what comes out is clear. Collect into a clean container and DISINFECT IT by boiling, chemicals or SODIS. Rinse or replace the sand and charcoal when flow slows or the water stops clearing. Germs build up in it.

The sun evaporates moisture under a plastic sheet. It condenses on the underside and drips into a container. The condensed water is distilled, so it's free of salt and usually free of germs. Honest yield Realistic yield is small, often a few hundred mL per day per pit. It is not a primary water source. In heat you can sweat out more digging the pit than it gives back, so dig in the cool of the day. Moisture condenses under the sheet, runs down to the low point and drips into the container.

s: pit, container, sheet, stone
f: Build it, step by step pit, container, sheet, stone
t: Pick a sunny spot with damp-looking soil if possible, such as a low area or a dry stream bed. Dig a bowl-shaped pit about 1 m (3 ft) across and 60 cm (2 ft) deep. Set a container in the centre at the bottom. Add a drinking tube running from it out of the pit if you have one. Add moisture around (not into) the container: chopped green non-toxic plants, or salt water, urine or dirty water poured into the soil. Cover the pit with clear plastic. Seal the edges all round with soil and rocks so no vapour escapes. Put a small stone in the middle of the sheet so it sags into a cone, with the low point directly over the container but not touching it. Leave it. Drink through the tube so you don't open the still and lose the trapped moisture. Don't put fuel-contaminated water in a still. Some fuels evaporate and condense along with the water.

No home method fixes chemical contamination No home method removes fuel, heavy metals, pesticides, industrial chemicals or toxic algae toxins. Boiling can concentrate some of them. Find another source.

Fuel or oil sheen, a rainbow film on the surface. Chemical, fuel or solvent smell, or unusual foam. Dead fish or dead animals in or near the water. Mine drainage and tailings: orange, red or white-stained rocks, unnaturally clear or oddly coloured water, piles of crushed rock nearby. Agricultural run-off: below fields, feedlots and orchards (pesticides, fertiliser, manure). Below industry, dumps, roads after a spill, or wrecked vehicles. Floodwater: presume it's contaminated with sewage, fuel and chemicals. Don't drink it or wash dishes in it. Wash your skin after contact. Blue-green algae scum: water that looks like pea soup or spilled paint, green or blue-green streaks, or mats. Its toxins survive boiling. Keep pets and livestock away, because it can kill dogs quickly. Don't use it for cooking or bathing either. Instead: collect rain, find a spring, go upstream of the problem, or use stored water.

Use food-grade containers: water jugs or barrels made for drinking water, or PET drink bottles. Never use containers that held chemicals, fuel or non-food products. Avoid milk and juice jugs, which are hard to clean and break down. Wash with soap and water, then rinse. Sanitize: mix 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented bleach in 1 quart (about 1 L) of water. Pour it in, cap, and shake so it touches every inside surface. Wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out, then air-dry or rinse with safe water. Fill with safe water (treated, or from a safe tap). Don't touch the inside of the cap or neck. Label it "Drinking water" with the date. Store it cool and dark, away from fuel, pesticides and chemicals, whose vapours can pass through plastic. Rotate it about every 6 months. Use the old water for washing or cooking and refill. Pour, don't dip. Use a tap or a clean scoop. Never put hands or used cups into stored water.

Carry two methods, such as a filter plus tablets, or a stove plus tablets, in case one fails, freezes or runs out. Collect upstream of trails, camps, livestock and toilets. Bury human waste at least 200 ft (60 m) from water in a hole 6–8 in (15–20 cm) deep. Mark "dirty" and "clean" bottles. Don't let untreated water drip onto drinking threads or caps. Wash or sanitize your hands before eating and after the toilet. Many "water" illnesses actually come from hands. Cold weather: keep filters from freezing (sleep with them). Store bottles upside-down so ice forms at the bottom, not in the lid. Chemicals work slower in cold water, so give them longer and double the bleach dose. Where tap water isn't safe: use sealed bottled water or treated water for drinking, brushing teeth and ice. Hot drinks made with boiled water are fine. Plan your carry: know where the next reliable water is before you leave the last one.
